An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, when combining this result with the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ branching fraction, a 95% confidence level was achieved, resulting in an upper limit for the magnitude of the off-diagonal $B^0_s$ mixing parameter $\Delta\Gamma_{bs}/\Gamma_b$ at 6.2 × 10^-5. Additionally, when considering various scenarios for the ratio of the real and imaginary parts of the $\Delta\Gamma_{bs}/\Gamma_b$ parameter, a 90% confidence interval of -0.026 to 0.026 was determined for the former, influencing the latter to be within the range of -0.005 to 0.005. These outcomes hold valid assumptions about the $B^0_s$ decay into $K^+K^-$ being a spin-zero process and neglecting possible distortions from additional decay channels. As a result, the current measurement stands as the most precise yet reported for this parameter. Nonetheless, when comparing this measure to theoretical estimates derived from Lattice QCD at a higher precision level, a discrepancy remains. Efforts to further refine this measure are ongoing with enhanced data sets available from 2015 and forward. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the benefits of federated learning in this domain, we conducted an analysis of model performance using metrics that assess the accuracy of tumor cell detection and classification. Our results demonstrate that federated learning can yield models with high agreement rates with existing annotations, as well as low rates of false positives and negatives. To facilitate replication and advancement of our study, we are making available the code and model weights through open-source repositories. Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach on diverse time-series datasets, showcasing a marked improvement in the quality of activated models. The technique has two key benefits: (1) it facilitates efficient network design, and (2) it excels in adaptive network applications where datasets have varying time-series contents. The techniques we've proposed can also be applied to other convolutional networks, and we've made our code publicly available. Overall, our method delivers a high-optimal activation baseline that can be used as a benchmark for future research in efficient deep learning networks. The code can be found here: https://github.com/hjdwu/Dilated-Pruning. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. Additionally, this work introduces a new class of skew commutative algebras and explores their properties in a specific context. For a given field, we demonstrate that a specific family of free Zinbiel algebras exhibit nilpotency of a specific dimension, which provides further evidence for the algebra's dimensional growth pattern. A derivation approach is also utilized to offer a potential explanation for the algebra's behavior. Finally, we establish a connection between the algebras' solvability and nilpotency, and explore various properties of their central elements.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, this new technique paves the way for future studies on fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC with data from 2010 and onward, as well as in proton--proton and lead--lead collisions at lower energies, such as in collisions at $\sqrt{s_N M}= 27$ GeV. This new technique will allow for a deeper comprehension of the quark--gluon plasma's behavior and allow for comparisons with theoretical models that simulate the collisions' development. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse engineering of the ALBA algorithm for DLEs facilitates the computation of inductive formulas from their first-order correspondents, a previously unexplored capability. Moreover, this achievement is linked to a hereditarily anti-chain condition of the finite algebraic signature associated with the logic, and this property is both necessary and sufficient for the computation of an inductive formula. This development is an important extension of the established results for logics whose finite algebras are finite direct products of finite distributive lattices. Additionally, this research introduces a new algorithmic approach to computing the finite algebras associated with first-order correspondents of inductive formulas, and provides a related definition of computable elements within the context of DLEs. The proposed method is demonstrated through its application to logic with operators for epistemic reasons and belief revision. The associated software is publicly accessible and includes the ALBA reverse engineer in its latest version. The associated paper is currently under review for publication in the Journal of Logical and Algebraic Methods in Programming. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through practical applications. Moreover, we provide an implementation of our approach through a data table handler available in the data quality assessment toolkit. This research lays the groundwork for addressing inconsistencies in data tables and fosters further investigation into the underlying mathematical concepts and practical applications. The underlying concepts of this research have mathematical foundations tied to Four-valued logic and the algebra of deductive systems, facilitating the examination of pressing problems like data quality assessment, query validation, and data merging. The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Additionally, it highlights key design parameters and their associated challenges, covering aspects such as the tracking system's readout silicon pixels, the calorimeter system's development, the vertex detector's development, and particle flow analysis implementation. Furthermore, it outlines strategies for optimizing design parameters through ongoing R&D, emphasizing the importance of maintaining design parameters consistent with achievable technological advancements by the time of construction. This review aims to stimulate collaboration, inform development pathways, and provide a foundation for ongoing design parameter optimization. It is intended to be a living document, reflecting the evolution of design parameters as R&D progresses.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. Using the EAGLE cosmological simulation, our findings of a moderate alpha-enrichment, nitrogen spread, and low s-process enrichment were replicated in a region with minimal star formation slowing, further supporting the estimated large distance of the cluster. The moderate metal content and unique chemical characteristics of Tononzintla 2 make it a useful subject for studying the chemical evolution of distant rich-metallic galactic clusters. The availability of APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra for the cluster allows for additional investigations of Tononzintla 2 through new analysis methods such as stellar clusters velocity fields and star clusters chemical abundance profiles. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. To further investigate this observation, I plan to explore other key properties of the archive, including the distribution of citation counts and the co-development of related content within the Isabelle Archive, as well as examining evidence for the absence of clear distinctions between proof strategies and tactics in the Isabelle proof base, as indicated by clustering analyses. Additionally, I aim to enhance the archive's accessibility by developing an interactive visualization tool to map the underlying structure of the archive and inform readers on the web. As an additional aspect, I plan to apply the measures of redundancy and cover from information theory to gain insight into the efficacy of search strategies within the archive. As my research draws to a close, I hope to contribute a chapter to the field by presenting my findings, which, as the archive continues to evolve, has significant implications for how we search, understand, and use its content. As such, I also aim to contribute a tool that can be useful for readers to the Isabelle proof base, and, as a by-product, develop skills that can be applied to other large-scale formal proof repositories. Throughout this research, I plan to present my discoveries in the form of a thesis that can be defended publicly. As such, I will regularly share my progress with the Isabelle community via regular reports, anticipating feedback that can guide and enhance my research. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the

atoms, achieving results that rival the most effective existing methods in the field.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/ChenZhSui/Direct-Pose-Code. The paper's findings are showcased in the following video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H5s5D3H5T9E. The paper has been accepted by the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR'20).

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Moreover, it
includes an efficient implementation, robust testing capabilities, and useful
functions for model evaluation, such as the calculation of AIC and BIC scores. The package also allows for the visualization of estimation results, including confidence intervals for sparsity patterns and scatter plots of estimated variables and covariance structures. Furthermore, it includes an efficient batch implementation for large-scale applications, a user-friendly GUI for easy model selection, and an innovative strategy for model comparison called CORP. CORP enables the selection of the best-fitting model by clustering solutions from different initial conditions and evaluating model robustness. The package is highly versatile and is suitable for a wide range of applications, from small to large datasets. The source code for GGLasso is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Arellano82/GGLasso. The package is extensively tested on various real and synthetic datasets in the GGLasso_test directory. For further information, please refer to the accompanying user guide available at https://github.com/Arellano82/GGLasso_documentation. The package includes several demo scripts, particularly demo_graphical_lasso.R and demo_general_graphical_lasso.R, to illustrate its key features. The developers of the GGLasso package are open to feedback and look forward to receiving suggestions for enhancing the package. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Consequently, this method may provide a critical boost to molecular dynamics simulations, making it suitable for a broader range of applications and enabling the exploration of time scales that were previously inaccessible. Additionally, this method allows for increased sensitivity to energy barriers, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of molecular processes. As a result, this method deserves serious consideration for adoption in biomolecular simulations. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology. Though the two materials performed similarly in terms of acoustic properties, the Stycast lens had the advantage of withstanding higher temperatures and pressures. This suggests that Stycast 1090SI has the potential to become a popular choice for designing acoustic lenses. To facilitate replication of our study, detailed manufacturing guidelines for PMMA and Stycast lenses have been provided. Ultimately, our research indicates that Stycast 1090SI offers a practical solution for reducing distortion in acoustic lenses.

By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both objective and subjective evaluations on real-world images. The model's code is available at https://github.com/zwang57/RAW-SSDA.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. These findings have been obtained through the use of high-speed imaging technology in experiments involving spheres entering water at various speeds. In some cases, the results were compared with computer simulations, revealing minor discrepancies, especially when modeling intermediate-speed pinch-off times. In general, however, our empirical rules provide a useful basis for enhancing the understanding of and improving models of the water-entry process. Furthermore, our research has revealed the importance of distinguishing between water-entry stages and the need to refine current models by taking into account the role of pressure within the cavity. Lastly, our work has shown that the surface-seal regime shares key characteristics with other water-entry stages, despite initial perceptions that it would behave differently. In fact, the surface-seal regime has been found to exhibit a unique two-phase pinch-off process, involving both partial-seal and secondary pinch-off stages, and requiring further investigation. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of the water-entry process will depend on continuing to explore the complex interactions between spheres and water upon impact, as well as the subtle yet critical differences that exist across various speed ranges. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

Finally, we outline possible pathways for further optimizing performance and integrating more intricate security mechanisms. 

Our research, representing an early exploration of the domain-based hardware concept, is realized through collaboration with industry partners and built on the Zephyr OS and Linux for the hardware components. 

Our study paves the way for reevaluating smartphone design under a security-first lens and encourages broader exploration of this novel hardware approach. 

We are also providing our research findings and constructions in the form of ready-to-use software and reproducible experiments for the security community to build upon and evaluate in greater detail.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain robust policies comparable to those obtained using the natural policy gradient method with substantial cleaning of data. We also provided theoretical and practical aspects of robust reinforcement learning, offering several directions for further research. The code for the FPG algorithm has been made available online.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Notably, the orbital selectivity in cubanite can be modified by the intense mixing of d and s states in its molecular iron ions, giving rise to a unique situation where the charge transfer and crystal field contributions have opposing effects on the system's behavior. This has the result of eliminating both on-site Hund's coupling and neighboring iron ion's orbital ordering, thus explaining the compound's distinct magnetic and structural properties. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the unique properties of cubanite and identifies the potential for orbital selectivity to serve as a universal parameter for this kind of material. This concept is then applied to other members of the malonite family. This analysis is carried out through a comparison with experimental data and tailored theoretical models, allowing for a clear illustration of the way the molecular structure's near-atomic details influence its macroscopic properties. This study also highlights the need for a careful examination of the orbital composition of iron ions within these compounds, given the common practice of treating them as averages. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we propose implementing a cavity to improve detection efficiency by reducing loss and controlling photon loss through the catalysis process. Our research provides a comprehensive examination of SPCCSs, encompassing their generation, fundamental properties, and utilization in complex scenarios involving continuous-variable measurement interactions. These states offer a promising platform for exploring quantum optics with continuous variables and creating robust non-classical states of light. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how bivectors can be utilized to develop a method for generating complex self-dual gravitational field equations in flat space, described by the Minkowski basis. Consequently, this enables the recovery of both the self-dual and anti-self-dual components of the electromagnetic field. In addition, we establish relationships between the Minkowski basis and the complex null tetrad basis, revealing the fundamental principles of spin duality. Finally, we conclude by discussing the implications of establishing the Gravitational Hodge Star Operator in the context of the Newman-Penrose formalism. This includes the understanding that it is possible to define the gravitational Hodge star operator across both self-dual and anti-self-dual components. Nevertheless, we observe that this is achievable solely within the context of the complex null tetrad basis, the Gravitational Hodge Star Operator cannot be defined across both self-dual and anti-self-dual components in the full algebra of the Weyl tensor. This limitation originates from the inherent properties of the complex null tetrad basis, allowing for the separation of the algebra of the Weyl tensor into self-dual and anti-self-dual components. Consequently, this analysis leads to the derivation of the gravitational Hodge star operator in the context of the complex null tetrad basis, resulting in the definition of the Kershaw matrix. This review offers a fresh perspective on the established theory and provides a new framework for understanding complex self-dual gravitational field equations in flat space, described by the Minkowski basis. Moreover, this framework enables the recovery of both the self-dual and anti-self-dual components of the electromagnetic field. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. However, the method's ability to perform safely and efficiently relies on the correctness of a sensitivity matrix that needs minimal adjustments whenever changing the forward model. Therefore, to utilize LM-EnRML in real field settings, it is necessary to develop a correct sensitivity matrix for the appropriate formation evaluation problem. The proposed method can be applied to other problems solvable by gradient-based methods such as EnKF. The code is available upon request for further research collaboration. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, our evaluations reveal significant enhancements in nested NER precision, especially within deeply nested scenarios. We express obstacles to counting these curves and their associated tangencies by altering the structure of these curves and their starting properties, focusing on edges and how they are affected. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using this new method in conjunction with the ZigBee network's data transmission process. We observe that implementing this location detection method causes a significant increase in energy consumption, however, to determine its potential in real-world applications, we need to conduct more tests with larger, more complex setups. The development of a mobile node detector application has also been completed, and we are now in a position to investigate the location detection method's effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By accelerating the development of multilingual models, we can better serve the needs of diverse, ever-expanding communities in the NLP domain. This work aims to spark progress and guide potential researchers in addressing challenges and opportunities within this field. It also introduces a code repository that includes code examples, benchmarks, and guidelines for evaluating code-mixing models. The study is conducted under the umbrella of the recently introduced MultiLingXL model family by the authors. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, human descriptions of images's semantic contents could be generated through a visual grounding approach using lightweight models. Another possibility is to utilize visual classification and object detection tasks' results to develop more practical description evaluation metrics. Ultimately, we need a human-based scoring standard that would streamline the development and evaluation of image description systems, making progress more transparent and comparable across different architectures and datasets. This score should be affordable to human subjects, clear in its guidelines, and consistent in its assessment of diverse description types. A basic starting point for such a standard could be developed using the existing large-scale data sets, and I propose testing this standard's validity through a controlled experiment. This experiment would involve recruiting naive human subjects to evaluate actual image descriptions generated by a simple baseline model, and I would examine the correlation between these human ratings and the similarity metrics used previously. This standard could potentially serve several purposes, such as informing the design of more effective description generation models, contributing to the development of best practices for this task, and facilitating more realistic evaluation of models in real-world applications. Additionally, I believe this standard could also be used to guide the development of other visual language models, such as those that generate captions from sentences rather than images. This is particularly relevant because, as I will show in Section 5, captions generated by these models are often similar to descriptions of images's semantic contents, which suggests they may benefit from evaluation standards similar to those proposed here. To summarize, this paper proposes a new evaluation standard for image description systems and discusses several alternatives to human-generated reference data. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This research has successfully identified the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure and confirmed its unique features through theoretical simulations. It has also provided a basis for better understanding the chemical compound both in its bulk and nanoparticle forms. Consequently, this research can serve as a model for studying other complex materials. It has a broader significance, as it has also highlighted the capability of time-dependent density functional methods to study reflection loss functions accurately. It has been previously believed that such methods were only suitable for simple systems only. It has now been proven that they can be applied to a wide range of complicated materials as well. It is hoped that this research will encourage a thorough investigation of Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticle properties, which could lead to development of new applications, such as hadron therapy cancer treatments. It is also believed that the theoretical approaches used here can be adapted for studying other oxide compounds, such as strontium and calcium titanates, that exhibit similar complex structures. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only communities exhibiting extreme values on these dimensions exhibited increased dissemination of misinformation. Our findings suggest that effective misinformation reduction strategies should account for underlying cultural factors in those communities. We also introduced the Information Convergence Model to illustrate the relationships between misinformation dissemination, population size, culture, geography, and technology. The model highlights the challenges in combating misinformation due to the underlying currents of public opinion. To validate our findings, we conducted additional experiments using different data sets and alternative analysis methods. Nonetheless, we acknowledge limitations to our study, including the reliance on anonymous online comments, which may not represent the broader population in each state. Nonetheless, our research provides a initial framework for examining the dissemination of misinformation in geographical regions. The source code for our analysis is available under a permissive license. We also introduced the Infofacts platform to present and refine our findings visually. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile detection framework that is adaptable to various applications and data streams. Furthermore, we highlight potential pathways for enhancing the algorithm in response to evolving digital challenges.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that speech content is relatively consistent across different vocabulary options available to humans, which may be a beneficial area for further exploration in this domain. By better understanding the characteristics of audio input from human instructors, we can develop more effective approaches to learning from demonstrated tasks. This, in turn, has the potential to enhance robotic performance by leveraging the full range of audio feedback from its human operators. This research paves the way for a more comprehensive exploration of this topic, offering other experts a clear direction on what aspects to investigate, which can lead to the development of more precise models for analyzing audio data in this context. These models can then learn to recognize important patterns in speech, such as identifying key vocabulary used to describe specific task elements, to support the learning process. This study provides a foundational framework for exploring the relationship between speech patterns and their associated actions, which can be refined and extended to cover a broader range of actions and tasks. To facilitate further research, we are making available a dataset featuring speech input from humans instructing a robot using spoken language across various tasks. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Our study thus provides a clear, self-contained overview of fundamental concepts underlying our proposed framework. A key aspect involves demonstrating how complexity properties can be accurately described through Euler-Arnold equations and its integro-differential generalizations, highlighting the importance of robust optimization techniques for both theoretical and practical understanding. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Despite these challenges, we have made progress in creating a simple proof system for reasoning about the behavior of conversational systems and implementing basic tools for automated testing, including a theorem prover and a model checker. We have also designed elements of a testing language, such as methods for asserting expected system responses and diagnosing faults emerging during testing. While our current framework is primitive, we believe it represents a starting point for further exploration into the unique testing challenges posed by conversational systems. We have publicly available source code for our research, and encourage developers to contribute to and make use of this framework along with us. Alongside the code, we have published a paper that includes detailed technical aspects, and invite researchers and practitioners to join us in this research effort. Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties $\sigma_M$ associated with detecting a hypothetical "Planet X" by analyzing its impact on the gravitational field of the known planets. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered Earth or Mars-mass object should be detectable for more than 90% of the sky up to 260 and 120 AU, respectively. Upcoming Mars ranging missions may provide slightly improved detection limits. The project also explores the effectiveness of highly accurate astrometry (determining positions and movements) of approximately 8000 Jovian Trojans from 2023 to 2035 using data from the upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).  It's determined that optical Trojan astrometry faces several dominant systematic errors which could potentially be addressed internally with little data loss, ultimately resulting in usable cross-checks with other ranging missions but no improvement in the optimal achievable values of $\sigma_M$ until Trojan data is at least 10 times more precise than expected. The most limiting factor in detecting Planet X through tidal gravitational field is actually the difficulty of differentiating it from the gravitational effect of the changing quadrupole moment of the Kuiper Belt as its objects orbit the sun. Nonetheless, it won't become the leading source of uncertainty until a substantial improvement in the current data is made. The project also considers various alternative approaches to detecting Planet X, including searching for signs of gravitational influence on the orbit of the Sun, looking for subtle patterns in the solar system's precession caused by X's presence, examining if X could be identifying itself as a massive object passing in front of a background field of X-rays, and finding evidence of X causing instability in the solar system's stability boundary, ultimately concluding that these methods face significant challenges until a substantial improvement is made in reducing $\sigma_M$. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/XLM-TM.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, we cannot confirm the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Additionally, we discovered that our findings rely heavily on the use of multivariate data analysis, and we urge future investigations to explore this approach as well. Lastly, we highlight the need for further investigation into the characteristics of low-variance circles and Hawking points, as well as the mechanisms that could give rise to local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB. Lastly, we propose that the scientific community should undertake a comprehensive analysis of the CMB using HawkingNet, and make the results publicly available, in order to provide a clear understanding of the implications for fundamental theories. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR promotes a unified perspective on CDR, addressing data sparsity in each participating domain rather than isolating user preferences within each domain. Moreover, the concise and transparent architecture of MSDCR facilitates rich feature extraction and alleviates over-fit concern, respectively. Additionally, the versatile framework of MSDCR is applicable to various multi-target CDR scenarios. The code and data of MSDCR are openly available at {https://github.com/} for further research. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The development also includes an easy-to-use toolkit allowing users to create their own exotic cones and to generate the simplified formulations used by Hypatia. This toolkit can also be used to create custom interior-point solvers. Hypatia is particularly notable for its superior performance when applied to certain large-scale optimization problems. The development is compatible with both CPLEX and GUROBI, and is available under the MIT License on the JuliaJuliaOpt GitHub repository. The source code for this paper is available online at https://github.com/JuliaOpt/HypatiaJuliaOpt-Hypatia, where users can find the code for the examples presented in this paper, as well as instructions for installing and utilizing Hypatia. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes highlight crucial considerations for developing and employing automated quality control methods in MRI analysis for research projects. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our findings also give us insights into the ordered generating sequences of the finite dihedral group Dn, specifically for its odd members. Furthermore, our work gives a special perspective on the ordered generating sequences of the free group on two generators, Fa, Sa, which reveals their intricate structure. We demonstrate that every element within Fa, Sa can be expressed as a product of powers of a, s, arranged in a specific order, which we refer to as the standard ordered generating sequence. This enables us to establish a link between the standard ordered generating sequences and the free reduction rules, which we use to derive a novel representation of the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn. This representation allows us to investigate various properties of the standard ordered generating sequences, which gives us valuable insights into the structure of the free group Fa, Sa. Lastly, our findings give us a method to monitor the movement of elements within the free group Fa, Sa, which is comparable to the approach used to analyze the movement of elements within the symmetric group Sn, as described by R. Shwartz. Our study offers a novel perspective on the standard ordered generating sequences of non-abelian groups and sheds light on the complex structure of the free group Fa, Sa. It also introduces a new approach to examining the structure of groups that are locally of the free type, which is characterized by being a finite Coxeter group at a finite generation depth. Ultimately, this study sets the stage for investigating the standard ordered generating sequences of groups that are locally of the free type, which is a key area of research, according to M. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Still, its utility will depend on the outcome of subsequent investigations into potential biases introduced by this correction method. Nonetheless, this approach holds promise for optimizing the understanding of the Hubble constant and the characteristics of galactic dark matter haloes, all without requiring direct observational data on dark matter properties. This research also paves the way for exploring other gravitational lensing effects on SN Ia and incorporating this additional context in future analyses. As a byproduct of this study, we've established a framework for calculating the effects of foreground galaxies on SN Ia, involving a combination of vector and scalar fields that describe lensing consequences. Lastly, this work lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive investigation of the interplay between SN Ia, dark matter, and gravitational lensing, one that could provide a more precise understanding of the fundamental properties of the cosmos. This research has been made publicly accessible through a simple code module that can be incorporated into existing cosmological analyses using SN Ia data. This code is now integrated into the BoltCosser code package, an open-source implementation of exact relativistic distance calculations for SN Ia, and is available at http://github.com/AdrianLambas/BoltCosser-Code. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we demonstrate that a precise measurement of this asymmetry can provide valuable insights into the spin-dependent dihadron fragmentation function and facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of hadron spin structure. Furthermore, we propose using the charge structure of sidebands as an effective method to distinguish true dihadron production from combinatorial background in SIDIS. This strategy is expected to significantly improve the accuracy of measurements related to the dihadron fragmentation function. Finally, we suggest measuring the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in inclusive dijet production at the EIC, which can provide additional evidence for the existence of twist-4 dijet fragmentation functions. Overall, we expect that experimental measurements at the EIC, JLab 12 GeV, and COMPASS will significantly enrich our knowledge of the dihadron fragmentation function and the spin structure of the proton. Consequently, these measurements will have a major impact on our preparation for future experiments, such as the PANDA at FAIR, where detailed studies of the spin structure of the proton are planned. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Following this discovery, Springer was able to develop a rigorous proof that the number of conjugacy classes in Sp_n(K) is equal to the product of the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree d over K and the number of pairs (e1, e2) where e1 and e2 are non-negative integers that sum to 2 and are subject to certain constraints. Notably, this result provides a novel formula for the class number of Sp_n(K), giving insight into a long-standing conjecture of George Lusztig. Furthermore, this development enables the derivation of a refined formula for the index of the center in Sp_n(K), yielding specific expressions for certain values of n and various fields K. Additionally, this work leads to a significant breakthrough in understanding the structure of the Weyl group of Sp_n(K) through its connection to the symmetric group S_d over K, enabling the description of conjugacy classes within a basis of the Lie algebra of Sp_n(K) in the form of combinations of varying Hermitian forms and quadratic forms. This foundation further enables the identification of specific elements within the Weyl group, including those associated with the ADL (Arithmetic, Dynamics, Geometry) framework. This translation becomes the second chapter of van der Kallen's 1967 Ph.D. thesis, obtained under the supervision of C.P. Mummert. This research was initiated by Springer's work but also incorporated additional contributions, especially involving the refinement of the class number of Sp_n(K) and the index of the center in Sp_n(K). It ultimately resulted in the derivation of conjugacy classes within a basis of the Lie algebra of Sp_n(K), leading to connections between these classes and various Hermitian forms and quadratic forms. This translation has now been reviewed for accuracy.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these challenges, we propose the use of adversarial techniques and neural networks for the representation of individual word distributions, also exploring the extension of these methods to sentence-level embeddings. Our research paves the way for a more precise disentanglement of word distributions in NLP, enabling better comprehension of the underlying mechanisms and capabilities of these widely applied models. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Aiming to apply this to actual linguistic data, our method includes a means to compute the spin state corresponding to a sentence's interpretation, enabling the selection of the most likely interpretation in cases of ambiguity. Furthermore, our technique enables the expression of the probability distribution associated with a sentence's interpretations, enabling the evaluation of the sentence's likelihood of conforming to specific contextual norms. The proposed method is demonstrated through the analysis of a logically simple but semantically complex sentence: "The author of the book being discussed is female". Our method successfully computes the spin state representing the sentence's interpretation and shows the associated probability distribution. The complexity of the algorithm necessitates its implementation using the HOPLAST parser, a highly optimized parser for a simplified version of the extended Lambek Calculus. The computed spin state can be viewed as the sentence's interpretation, enabling the discharge of contextual norms specified in the context of the sentence.
