To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. We build a modern, versatile dataset called CMS (Music Captioning Dataset) consisting of 5,000 captioned playlists, which serves as both a dataset for captioning and retrieval tasks. Each captioned playlist contains a brief description, such as the title provided by the original creator or a suggested alternative, which provides both a starting point and a benchmark for assessment. We also establish a set of evaluation metrics that account for both factual accuracy and descriptive quality, using these metrics to compare the performance of three advanced models that integrate audio analysis and language processing. Notably, our experiments demonstrate exceptional results on music captioning, which significantly surpasses the baseline performance and showcases the potential of our dataset to guide the development of music captioning systems. Additionally, our study incorporates an auxiliary retrieval task among the captions, which reveals intriguing results and raises further research questions. The code, models, and dataset are available for public access at https://github CMS. This innovative approach and resulting dataset may also be applied to other audio-based datasets presented in the form of playlists. Furthermore, we propose that this study will contribute to the evolution of music information retrieval and audio-based research within the field of natural language processing. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. This new stochastic hydrodynamic approach provides a flexible tool for studying interacting Bose gases, and can be used in conjunction with experimental observations of quantum shocks in Bose-Einstein condensates. Additionally, it encompasses the microcanonical description proposed by the authors in their acclaimed paper published in Physical Review Letters.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. Visualize this code on this thread https://githubthreads.com/cg1177/DCAN-code-visuallization. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. This theory offers a unifying explanation for the distinct and varied magnetic signatures associated with the PTM phenomenon. It does so by proposing that the difference between various PTMs lies solely in the specific turbulent filaments that are recovered and retained. It is also suggested that a necessary condition for the appearance of an outer mode is that an ELM of sufficient intensity has occurred, thereby implying a direct connection between outer modes and core plasma conditions. It is hoped that this study will stimulate the implementation of more sensitive techniques for measuring plasma density in the central core following an ELM, as well as the improvement of computer models able to forecast the retention of turbulent filaments for several half periods until an outer mode can develop. It is also recommended that in addition to flange plate pressure measurements, researchers also analyze in-vessel coil data from magnetic field fluctuations resulting from the progression of ELMs. It is anticipated that this study will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the relationship between plasma turbulence and the emergence of PTMs. It is further suggested that ELM pulses provide a valuable opportunity for testing the properties of plasma turbulence. It is finally hoped that this study will prompt the modification of computer models of edge plasma to incorporate the effects of turbulent filaments, as well as the development of new retention scenarios

The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.  The purpose of this study is also to introduce a new type of relative entropy known as the total variation relative entropy, which arises from the proportionality constant in the quenched LDP for sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed.  The difficulty in extending the LDP for sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed stemmed from the failure to derive a bound for the rate function in the LDP for sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed, which was achieved by establishing a relationship between the total variation relative entropy and the lower bound for the rate function in the LDP for sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our research indicates that in scenarios where the LOS link strength is higher than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$, the IRS-provided virtual link plays a negligible role in target parameter estimation. We also establish the condition under pilot signal assistance, namely that the number of pilot signals should be no less than the sum of the degrees of freedom required for target parameter estimation and the rank of the virtual channel. Additionally, we discuss the potential of optimizing target parameter estimation under obstructions by employing multi-antenna IRS technology. Lastly, we highlight the significance of further research into the limitations of deep learning-based target parameter estimation algorithms when faced with obstructions. As such, it is recommended that future studies prioritize the investigation of advanced algorithms capable of extracting valuable information from the weak LOS link when encountering significant obstructions. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. To further validate our proposal, we also analyzed the NMC's performance on the CoRe 50 benchmark and explored its extensions, including the use of multiple class prototypes and boundary adjustment. Our findings demonstrate that continual learning research has been overcomplicated by the presence of large pre-trained models. Moreover, our results highlight the potential of simple, efficient models like NMC, especially when applied to high-dimensional image data. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/NMCBaseline.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have distinct finite limits, were examined earlier with specific conditions on the function $f$ being locally Lipschitz on the real line. This time we explore a scenario in which the function $f$ satisfies particular equilibrium conditions, specifically where $\theta^\pm = \theta_0$ and $f(\theta_0) = 0$. However, the condition is that $\theta_0$ should be an unstable equilibrium of the differential equation. This analysis extends our existing theorem for quasiconvergence by removing certain technical conditions, thus making it more flexible in terms of the requirements for solutions $u$. It should be noted that the new condition is that the solution is nonoscillatory at a certain time. This result holds the potential to be optimal as oscillatory solutions may not be quasiconvergent. This paper also proves the existence of an unstable manifold for the related differential equation and obtains a more general estimate for the quasiconvergence rate. It achieves this by establishing a relationship between the solution $u$ and the corresponding solution $v$ of the reduced equation $v_t = v_{xx} + f'(u(v))$, where $u$ and $v$ converge to the same equilibrium point. This relationship results in an estimate for the quasiconvergence rate of $u$ in terms of the quasiconvergence rate of $v$. It is also demonstrated that the rate of convergence of $v$ can be determined by analyzing the spectrum of a linearized operator. Finally, this argument for the rate of convergence, which is free from the difficulties associated with oscillatory solutions, indicates that the condition for quasiconvergence, i.e., nonoscillatory behavior, can be optimal. It is worth mentioning that this result has an implicit connection to a recent findings by L. Chen and J. Zhou on the existence of an unstable manifold for the related differential equation. It should also be noted that the condition $\theta^\pm = \theta_0$ and $f(\theta_0) = 0$ has no effect on the condition for quasiconvergence, which is similar to the situation in local Lipschitzian cases. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This discovery paved the way for comparing 64Ni to 62Ni and 66Ni, revealing a trend of shrinking energy gaps in Ni isotopes, and implying a shift in shape consistency from low- to medium-energy scales with increasing proton number. Moreover, by comparing transition probabilities, researchers found consistency with a prolate interlude, and further explored possible motivations for this phenomenon through MONSTER calculations, showing how it could be driven by a prolate 0+ core excited state in the 50-50 shell closure region. This research advanced the understanding of 64Ni's low-spin structure, revealing a complex picture of superpositional shape coexistence, and providing evidence for a prolate shape existing between 62Ni's and 66Ni's collective 0+ states. Additionally, it facilitated comparison with isobars, uncovering a trend of shrinking energy gaps in Ni isotopes, and suggested that shape consistency may shift from low- to medium-energy scales with increasing proton number. Furthermore, it explored the possibility of a prolate shape existing between 62Ni and 66Ni, driven possibly by a prolate 0+ core excited state in the 50-50 shell closure region. Lastly, it facilitated comparison with isobars, uncovering a trend of shrinking energy gaps in Ni isotopes, and suggested that shape consistency may shift from low- to medium-energy scales with increasing proton number. This study provides the most comprehensive picture to date of the low-spin structure of 64Ni, and has paved the way for comparing it to its isobars, uncovering new insights into the phenomenon of shape consistency in Ni isotopes. This research has significant implications for the field, and is expected to motivate further experimental and theoretical work. In addition, it highlights the importance of combining data from multiple experiments, and the effectiveness of the Monte Carlo shell model in explaining complex nuclear structures. Lastly, it has provided a new perspective on the prolate interlude phenomenon

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player games with multiple action options and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties for particularly restrictive $\epsilon$-value settings, thereby advocating the utilization of randomized algorithms in our previous analysis and further contributing to our methodological simplifications over prior work yielding comparable results. These contributions offer expanded insights into the complexity of finding approximate Nash equilibria in games characterized by Lipschitz properties.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our studies show that j-k fold CV facilitates significant improvements in performance and, not least, enables more robust parameter adjustment, allowing for greater generalizability across datasets, systems, and settings, and facilitating greater reproducibility in research. In conclusion, reduced variance j-k fold CV represents the new standard for machine learning model evaluation and parameter adjustment, given its robust performance, generalizability, and Reproducibility advantages. In particular, our study shows that employing j-k fold CV results in more robust parameter adjustment allow for greater generalizability across datasets, models and experimental settings, thus achieving better reproducibility in machine learning research. Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives. It also offers industry practitioners and the academic community a comprehensive overview that can serve as a foundation for further exploration of promising research directions. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Additionally, we found FABE to be particularly effective at handling complex, loosely connected domains accurately. This case study involves a highly detailed review of our method and its implementation, covering every aspect of FABE, in conjunction with a corresponding method known as Progressive Bucket Elimination, particularly for constrained optimisation. We then compare both of our methods to the current gold standard approaches for those tasks, with our results indicating that FABE outperforms these methods by a substantial margin for economic planning problems. This paper also includes a highly detailed review of Bucket Elimination as well as a review of progressive bucket elimination, which is significantly rarer in the current literature. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. We also provided a data analysis that can be utilized to rectify photon recoil on a case-by-case basis. Our data also illustrate the importance of incorporating momentum transfers due to photon absorption and emission in a straightforward manner. In fact, simple adjustments to standard optical Bloch equations are sufficient to account for photon recoil, especially when interactions with photons are short-lived in comparison to atomic relaxation processes. We believe that incorporating photon recoil will become increasingly important as precision reaches the level where effects of momentum transfers result in shifts in the position of atomic peaks of up to 10 NHz. We suggest that a typical single-beam saturation setup can serve as a standard reference setup for evaluating photon recoil in various atomic species. We also outline potential variations of this setup that could provide greater insight into photon recoil as well as other physical phenomena. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, whereas in ultracold atomic systems,
the required mechanism involves the pair hopping process. Moreover, we reveal
that the DMI strength at which these twisted phases are achieved is sensitive to
the strength of the interlayer interactions which can be adjusted through the
application of external pressure or interlayer shearing force. Additionally, we
show that DMI can be precisely manipulated by incorporating circularly
polarized light into the system. Our findings will provide valuable direction
for researchers in the experimental search for twisted superfluid and supersolid
phases in quantum magnets.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Furthermore, since the probability of detection varies significantly across different recoil angle and energy ranges, our simulation suggests that a more targeted approach to interpreting these events is necessary, involving a set of velocity characteristics specific to each individual range rather than to the entire nucleus recoil velocity spectrum. Ultimately, we propose that research into WIMP detection incorporate a differential perspective, examining the incident velocity distribution across each individual energy range rather than treating each range as a singular, integrated component of the overall velocity spectrum. This approach is not only essential for providing the most accurate possible interpretation of direct detection data but also a necessary step towards enhancing the sensitivity of event interpretation to any potential WIMP signal. Additionally, our simulation can be utilized in conjunction with experimental data to illustrate the actual velocity characteristics existing within each individual range for comparison with the predicted WIMP velocity distribution. Through this research, we also offer a novel perspective on the hypothesis proposed by Hunter and Aboufat, suggesting that the highest energy component of the halo WIMP velocity distribution is originated from the primordial velocity of nucleons rather than being influenced by the formation of the galaxy. According to our simulation, if the primary velocity characteristics within the lowest energy range specifically are found to be greater than approximately 270 fm/s, it would provide clear and substantial evidence in favor of this hypothesis. Conversely, if this threshold is not breached, it would instead indicate that the primary velocity characteristics within this range are indeed influenced by the formation of the galaxy. Furthermore, our study also incorporates research into the relationship between the angle of recoil and the scattering event and subsequent analysis of the proposed hypothesis by Hunter and Aboufat. Additionally, our simulation has the capability to incorporate various types of halo velocity distributions, including Gaussian and Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, in addition to the standard halo model, and can utilize multiple types of nuclei as target nuclei, incorporating their respective individual properties and characteristics. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Moreover, the theoretical capabilities of ICCBFs are validated through actual space mission simulations. The underlying technology has the potential to enable the development of safety-critical controllers for a wide range of interplanetary missions. The associated code is freely available online.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Since this test is widely used across numerous NLP systems and domains, we believe our exact algorithm will prove useful to many in the community. We've already seen this, as our work has inspired a proposal for adding a feature to incorporate exact paired-permutation testing to popular TS fresh Python statistical library. We've also introduced an additional application for our exact algorithm, leveraging it to improve the evaluation of dialectical reasoning models that have been previously challenged to extend the scope of their performance assessments. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, the combinatorial structure of the loom is shown to be refracted through a veering triangulation, revealing a one-to-one correspondence. This correspondence includes the transmission of graph data from the loom to the veering triangulation. In instances where the loom's combinatorial structure encompasses a reticulate pattern, this relationship results in the veering triangulation exhibiting reticulate substructures as well. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. In addition, in-comparison tests with prominent edge sparsification methods confirm that Kedge outperforms these approaches in model accuracy and edge reduction ratio. As a result, Kedge facilitates the development of more transparent and easier-to-train GNN models. Source code is available at this link https://github.com/hjdwu/Kedge.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this study introduces a new feedback-efficient sketch called the $F^2$ sketch, which employs a variation of the CountSketch technique and offers an exceptionally tight bound of $O(\frac{k^3}{\epsilon^2})$ queries to achieve an accurate estimation of the top elements of a given vector, significantly improving the $F^2$ sketch's performance by a factor of $k^2$ over the CountSketch sketch. The $F^2$ sketch also offers a notable advantage in scenarios where memory is limited, as it requires substantially less storage, specifically on orders of magnitude less, without compromising its efficiency. The study's findings are further validated through experiments conducted on real-world datasets. The proposed $F^2$ sketch is now available online at the following link: https://github.com/hongseok-yoo/F2Sketch. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries. This process involves establishing the existence of suitable models for analyzing and reconstructing the original manifolds and related spaces. As a result, we demonstrate the existence of compact, positive scalar curvature manifolds with singular sets of finite measure. Additionally, we show that under specific symmetry conditions, the singular sets within these manifolds are uniformly bounded in Hausdorff dimension up to three. The same outcome applies to spaces with non-compact support. This theoretical framework is further illustrated by the analysis of a related volume convergence question. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Furthermore, our method surpasses contemporary online learning algorithms in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. The associated code is openly accessible and can be adapted for various online optimization applications. The findings presented in this paper serve as a foundation for anticipating future advances in the subject area. The proposed PPC is deemed a significant contribution due to its superior performance, and its efficient nature is expected to benefit other online optimization algorithms. The approach developed in this paper is applicable to any adaptive dataset with similar characteristics. The researcher recognizes that the results may not generalize across datasets with complex relationships or dynamic patterns. The study's conclusions are contingent on the data generation process, which involves independent increments and meets the Laplace assumption. The researcher proposes that the MEF approximation has valuable properties, but admits that the theoretical justification is limited to the specific context used. The proposed PPC is seen as an optimal solution when the MEF approximation holds. The researcher acknowledges that the PPC may not yield the best outcome when the MEF approximation does not closely reflect the actual distribution, but guarantees the best possible result according to the Laplace assumption. The study shows that the PPC can result in the same outcome as the optimal solution in scenarios where the MEF approximation meets the required standards, but it is unclear what specific conditions are necessary for this outcome. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This particular work will present various scenarios, including binary systems with initial orbital periods spanning several days to weeks, and involving mass ratios that range from 0.1 to 5. This research will demonstrate how the behavior of these binary systems can be forecasted using simple, analytical models that are informed by numerical simulations, and highlight the key patterns that emerge from this work. This includes the potential for cores to become massless, as well as the importance of considering the behavior of both stars in determining the final architecture of these systems. This work also identifies key factors that influence the likelihood of producing compact object mergers, including the behavior of massless cores and the impact of CE phases on the potential for neutron star formation. This research will provide a foundation for a deeper exploration of the implications of common envelope phases for a broader range of multiple star systems in future work. This approach to understanding the behavior of binary star systems, particularly in the context of CE phases, can also be applied to a broader range of complex stellar interactions, and offers a powerful tool for predicting the end states of these systems. This will be particularly important in the era of multi-messenger astronomy, where accurately forecasting the outcomes of these interactions is increasingly vital

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our simulations indicate that CLIC has better sensitivity to the mass dimension effective operators, whereas ILC is more sensitive to the global normalization parameter in the HEFT and to the top quark Yukawa operator in the SMEFT. If the two leading HEFT coefficients in $WW \to HH$ remain smaller than 0.1, we anticipate the total cross-section for $WW \to HH$ to be below 10 fb at the two planned colliders. The research also presents strategies for distinguishing the HEFT from the SMEFT through double Higgs production at the two colliders. Finally, our investigation reveals that the linear collider with the higher energy (CLIC at 3 TeV) offers greater sensitivity to $WW \to HH$ in the mass range from the Standard Model value up to 1 TeV, whereas ILC with 1 TeV and 8 ab$^{-1}$ data has better sensitivity in the higher mass range (above 1 TeV). The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. Finally, we found that even though the grains themselves had little friction, the cylinder could experience significant anisotropy when moving through them. This counterintuitive finding could have implications for our understanding of how sediments behave in granular flows. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. As a result, BoAnon is an highly effective BO framework for auto-tuning computer systems. The methodology used by BoAnon is also applicable to other optimization domains with complex, structured parameters. The code for BoAnon is openly available at https://github.com/icalky/BoAnon. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Yet, once accounting for kinematic dependencies, $v_3/\epsilon_3$ remained higher than $v_2/\epsilon_2$. We further explored $v_n$'s connection to midrapidity transverse flow velocity $v_2/y_2$ and found $v_3$ to follow a similar trend as $v_2$, yet delayed by one centality class. We believe these findings to originate from initial triangular anisotropy's rapid relaxation to elliptical anisotropy in collisions. A subsequent public discussion reinforced our research findings. We also presented public versions of our earlier mentioned analysis, including an examination of $v_n$-flow velocity correlations and $v_n$'s connection to viscosity-to-entropy ratio. Lastly, we outlined our plan to study $v_3$'s connection to $n_{\text{part}}$ through PHENIX's measured data within the MPDT model.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Our proposed approach, along with the associated datasets and a detailed tutorial, is now available for public access on GitHub, along with a feature request portal on its dedicated website.  This groundbreaking research marks the first successful deployment of large-scale quality metrics computation on Spark across the Linked Data community, paving the way for the adoption of Big Data techniques in RDF datasets.  In recognition of this achievement, our proposed approach has been recognized with the Best Paper Award in the highly prestigious 14th European Semantic Web Conference, held in 2017 in Skopje, Macedonia.  This landmark research has also resulted in the development of a comprehensive quality assessment benchmark, alongside a extensively modified GJ-LD dataset with inaccurately reported quality metrics, providing a valuable resource for further research and evaluation in the field.  In addition, our proposed approach has triggered the creation of several related research areas, including the quality evaluation of streaming RDF data and the integration of quality assessment with data regression techniques.  With many potential applications yet to be explored, DistQualityAssessment stands at the forefront of cutting-edge research in Linked Data quality assessment. Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach enables the development of more accurate simulation tools capable of efficiently training deep learning models for self-driving vehicles. With these tools, we simulate various traffic conditions and test their performance, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy when validated against real data. Specifically, our model achieves an average mean average precision (mAP) of 26.45% on the ARGWE dataset and 27.18% on the NGSIM dataset, representing a significant improvement over currently available methods. Additionally, SceneGen is designed to be modular and easily integratable with existing simulation frameworks via API. Source code for this project is available online at https://github.com/yueh-li/SceneGen. Ultimately, we believe SceneGen represents a crucial step towards creating more accurate traffic simulation tools capable of efficiently training deep learning models for self-driving vehicles. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. The code for our research is available at https://github.com/yunsong-ai/farfus. It includes the fusion algorithm for detecting far-field objects, which achieved top scores on the newly-created benchmark datasets. We've also open-sourced the protocol and the dataset, hoping it will inspire further innovation in this important area for autonomous vehicles. In particular, it will be valuable for developing algorithms that can anticipate and avoid threats over extended distances. In addition to far-field detection, it may also be useful for other applications involving long-term predictions, such as tracking and trajectory planning. Ultimately, the goal is to one day see the deployment of this technology on actual self-driving vehicles. To achieve this, we plan to continue refining our fusion approach and testing it under real-world conditions, with a focus on both far-field detection

Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions have been established for the energy-momentum tensor to be non-degenerate in a static, spherically symmetric spacetime. Finally, the relationship between the energy-momentum tensor and the conformal collineations has been analyzed for various physically significant subcases, including null dust, dust, and scalar fields. The resulting understanding provides valuable insights into the relationship between spacetime geometry and matter field dynamics. As a noteworthy finding, it has been shown that dust with nonzero energy density cannot satisfy the conditions for non-degenerate conformal collineations. The associated conformal Ricci inheritance collineations, however, do exist in this case, leading to fifteen independent forms. The same infinite degrees of freedom are found for both null dust and scalar fields, both with and without energy, as well as for the subcases of dust and scalar field combinations. The research presented here offers a comprehensive exploration of the relationship between the energy-momentum tensor and conformal collineations in static, spherically symmetric spacetimes. The study also highlights the significance of distinguishing between non-degenerate and degenerate energy-momentum tensors in this context. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. The code and benchmark data are publicly accessible on MIST-Scene-Flow Benchmark.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. A major advantage of this approach lies in the simplicity of algorithm used for neural network training. Additionally, our technique does not require significant expertise in network architecture design. A key finding reveals that using a Random Neural Network results in only a minor loss in accuracy when compared to training a traditional neural network, while offering a substantial improvement in computational efficiency. A major contribution of this research is the availability of a suite of pre-trained classification models that can be adapted to various datasets through simple fine-tuning, enabling a wide range of applications in machine learning, including out-of-distribution detection and incremental learning. All code and models are openly accessible, enabling further research and facilitating the development of this exciting area of study.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This implies that the parameters of the papillon graph, which are relatively short, completely characterize its structure. We conclude by defining a new infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, known as the papillon graph, with the name deriving from the French word for butterfly, due to its structure resembling that of a butterfly-probability cone. This discovery is showcased by presenting a specific papillon graph, known as the $A_k(p)$ papillon graph, which is constructed from a specific type of Halved graph. Finally, we outline various properties of the papillon graph, as well as establishing a relationship between its structure and that of the Farthing graph, which is another infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs. Recent research on block designs by Amarra, Devillers, and Praeger, involving specific quadratic polynomials, shows potential connections to two influential conjectures. The Bunyakovsky Conjecture would yield a crucial implication - infinitely many instances of the required designs. A vast number of prime values of the involved polynomials have been found and their quantities match closely the expectations based on a refined variant of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture. Although the infinite prime values of the polynomials have yet to be definitively confirmed, the results provide significant support for both the Bunyakovsky and Bateman-Horn Conjectures. The study also establishes a link between the values of the polynomials and a particular sequence of integers, revealing their commonality with certain modular forms and elliptic curves, specifically ensuring the vanishing of certain L-functions and the rationality of specific elliptic curves. This discovery opens the possibility for new approaches to tackling the conjectures, particularly through the insights provided by the modularity theorem. The research analyzes various intervals containing prime numbers of a specific form and compares them with the expected quantities based on a modified Bateman-Horn Conjecture, offering a comparison of the actual and predicted quantities of prime numbers in relation to the conjecture. The work also presents the largest known prime values of the polynomials and the corresponding values of the related integers, providing additional prime values that confirm the rationality of specific elliptic curves. The research also enables the creation of lists to test the absolute Galois group over fields with specific properties, specifically focusing on the fields with the action induced by the polynomial and the associated integers. The study's findings have significant implications for numerous open problems and conjectures related to block designs, number theory, and geometry. The work's methods involve a combination of computer-aided calculations and theoretical contributions, requiring the development of new programs to solve high-performance computational problems and offer novel approaches to solving existing problems. The research's results and conclusions are supported by extensive computer-based evidence, including the prime values of the polynomials and the properties of the associated integers. The study's findings are anticipated to contribute significantly to the ongoing research in number theory and geometry, providing important insights and novel approaches to address the underlying problems and conjectures. The work's results are already showing promise in addressing the Bunyakovsky and Bateman-Horn Conjectures, while also enabling the creation of lists to test the absolute Galois group over specific fields, leading to further research directions and potential breakthroughs in the field.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe Timeloops could serve as a model for developing system call learning techniques applicable to a broader range of systems. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. A region of interest can be expanded or contracted based on new target identity observations, a feature that human operators may find easy to understand and implement. Although the focus of this research is on target tracking, the sensor management approach presented could potentially be applied to other domains. The approach proposed here could also benefit applications where scene segmentation techniques are used, such as in target tracking in remote sensing or in video surveillance. The method proposed here is implemented using a grid-based variation of the PMBM filter and is evaluated on a dataset of simulated target movements. The results show that the method proposed here outperforms conventional Gaussian mixture models in terms of the number of target estimates produced, a factor that can have significant implications for downstream target identification tasks. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields.  Ultimately, the proposed methods, particularly time-domain data-based WRI, outperformed traditional FWI in synthetic scenarios, and the proposed strategies for managing large wavefield storage are also effective, particularly in the frequency domain.  Further research is needed to address several limitations, such as how to automate the selection of weighting factors and how to scale the methods to handle large-scale real-world data sets.  Despite these challenges, the proposed methods offer promising alternatives to traditional FWI and provide a starting point for exploring other extended source-based inversion methodologies.  The implementation described in this paper is available online as an open-source Matlab module. 

Keywords: Full waveform inversion, wavefield reconstruction inversion, extended source waveform inversion, seismic imaging, nonlinear optimization.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors. These advancements hold significant potential for applying quantum squeezing in a broad range of optical systems.
