We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data, particularly from the Swift observation in 2008, shows significant variations in spin period, spectral type and spectral energy distribution. These differences suggest significant internal matter accumulation, leading to longitudinal motion and accretion disk fluctuations, resulting in dynamic spectral patterns and potential Pulsar Wind Neutron Star activity in IGR J19294+1816. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model also identifies different asymptotic states in the presence of external noise, which leads to a shift in the critical point to half loop dynamics driven by loop formation. Additionally, the model provides an explanation for the evolution of diverse species through the formation of loop dynamics, which facilitates geographic speciation driven by dispersal distance. The model further illustrates the influence of migration and noise on species competition through separate analyses, and finally, the model offers implications for understanding ecological and biological phenomena in lattice structures. The model's equations are solved analytically for stable states and theoretically for dynamic behavior, and the results are validated through numerical simulations. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations hold significant implications for models' performance and ability to comprehend dialogue language. Additionally, our research reveals that incorporating context into evaluation tasks enhances the magnitude of differences in performance among models. This work aims to guide the development of more effective, yet efficient, dialogue models that prioritize accurate encoder representations and facilitates further exploration of encoder-depth evaluation in dialogue language understanding. This is achieved by introducing a new benchmark consisting of 47 evaluation tasks for six distinct scenarios, alongside auxiliary objectives that facilitate enhanced performance and, thus, a deeper understanding of encoder representations in dialogue language models. Our findings also suggest that utilizing auxiliary tasks with context-aware evaluation tasks leads to enhanced performance and, thus, a deeper understanding of encoder representations in dialogue language models. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Our findings suggest that context-aware acoustic feature engineering plays a crucial role in speech synthesis. Moreover, by incorporating contextual semantic elements, fine-grained speech characteristics align with the overall tone, resulting in an overall superior synthesis quality. Human evaluations confirmed these results, indicating superior performance of MaskedSpeech over baseline systems in terms of naturalness and expressiveness. Additionally, perceptual analysis revealed that the context-aware system is capable of producing a wide range of prosody patterns. Unlike traditional synthesis systems, MaskedSpeech can produce different tones in response to varying sentence contexts, leading to increased diversity in prosody. Additionally, cross-entropy loss and a layer normalization technique contributed to the production of subtle sentence-level prosody. Human evaluations of multiple comparisons between context and non-context models revealed the context-aware system's ability to produce diverse prosody patterns. Furthermore, subjective evaluations conducted across different languages other than Chinese also demonstrated superior performance of the context-aware system. Overall, MaskedSpeech represents a significant step towards the development of paragraph-level speech synthesis that accurately captures the nuances of speech. Alongside the code and models discussed in this paper, additional related paragraph-level synthesis studies are also reviewed and contrasted with our findings. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we propose that retinal IKNM could
serve as an optimal model for studying the complex interplay between spatial diffusion, local retention mechanisms,
and global circulation in dense, developing tissues. By integrating mathematical models of diffusion with experimental
data, we suggest that the gradual shift in the dominant direction of nuclear migration across the retina can be
traced back to subtle variations in the behavior of nuclei during IKNM. Additionally, our analysis discloses that the
retinal area with randomly allocated nuclei follows a fractal pattern, and we suggest that this geometric organization
may result from the superimposition of similar patterns of nuclear migration across successive waves of IKNM. 
Overall, our findings using multi-scale imaging and mathematical modeling for analysis provide a comprehensive view
of the complex, coordinated behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM in the developing zebrafish retina.

Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This code optimization problem is effectively framed as a general convex minimization task, and several code patterns with desirable structure are proposed and evaluated in various image processing scenarios, demonstrating notable improvements in reconstruction accuracy. Moreover, high-quality code patterns derived through this approach have the potential to be incorporated into compressed sensing systems, enabling seamless image reconstruction without additional processing. This paves the way for the widespread adoption of compressed sensing technology in image acquisition processes, such as video and demosaicing. This approach is also applicable to other signal processing tasks that involve coded measurement analysis, such as magnetic resonance imaging and source localisation, among others. Numerous code patterns with desirable structure are presented, and the associated reconstruction results are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of this strategy. This code pattern design methodology is particularly useful in scenarios where the encoder and decoder have minimal communication, such as in wireless communication systems, where coded measurements must be transmitted back to the decoder for reconstruction. This research provides a valuable design framework for coding strategies in compressed sensing and will likely spark further interest in this area, leading to the development of various code patterns with complex structures. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, we recorded a neutron detection rate of around 50 per day, and measured the spectrum of super-neutrinofrom 4.6 to 4.8 GeV. We also observed neutrons associated with around 30% of cosmic-ray muons, and found that returning muons have a much lower neutron production rate compared to incoming muons. Furthermore, we detected neutrons from cosmic-ray muons at energies above 100 GeV, and are in the process of analyzing their spectrum. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. Additionally, the proof establishes the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros under the more stringent condition that 8192 doesn't equal 0 in the finite field F_2. The study further illustrates the connection between the behavior of these L-functions and the distribution of zeros of Dirichlet L-functions, leveraging the work of Dietmann and Diaz y Diaz for supportive data. A theoretical lower bound on the speed of convergence towards quantum unique ergodicity is also derived. A significant aspect of the study involves the introduction of a new, more versatile definition of landau-siegel zeros, encompassing a broader class of associated L-functions and specifically addressing the topic at hand with the adopted definition. The study distinguishes between "true" landau-siegel zeros and those referred to as "fake" landau-siegel zeros in this expanded context. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. However, our analysis suggests that even a very small transmission of 0.1 persons per hour from a super-spreader in a scenario where community transmission is slow would still result in a substantially elevated $R_0$ value of approximately 33, which could have important implications for the management of infectious outbreaks through isolation and under certain conditions of rapid indoor gathering. We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. Through
correlation studies, we also extract the form factor at zero virtuality, enabling
predictions for other decays. For $\eta_c \rightarrow \gamma\gamma$, our result
represents the first direct determination of the decay width. The new method
facilitates a comparison of data and lattice simulations for monoxides, without
depending on the shape of the form factor. This becomes particularly relevant
for systems with a significant difference in masses between particles, such as
$\eta_c\rightarrow \gamma\gamma$. The novel approach allows a direct connection
between theoretical predictions and future experimental measurements of monoxides
decaying to two photons. In the case of $\eta_c$, our result implies a very
small branching ratio to $\gamma\gamma$, i.e., $\mathcal{B}(\eta_c\gamma\gamma) < 4.5\%$,
which has significant implications for photon-based $\eta_c$ detection systems. 
This technique can be applied to a variety of processes involving photons and
leptons in final states. Additionally, we outline the possibilities for using
lattice QCD to inform the interpretation of monoxides detected via electron scans. 
In the context of $\eta_c$, we derive the form factor at zero virtuality, which
can be utilized to predict additional decay channels, yielding $\Gamma_{\eta_c \gamma \mu \bar{\mu}} = 69.1(1.6)(8)$ eV. 
This new method for calculating the decay width of hadrons into two photons, 
often necessary for electron scans, can also be applied to a broader range of 
processes, including those involving leptons

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through a series of Monte Carlo simulations of Gaussian ensemble, specifically the evaluation of finite-temperature properties of the spectrum and the behavior of the electronic density in presence of harmonic potentials in quantum mechanics. Our method facilitates an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational resources required, paving the way for applying importance sampling to the most demanding scenarios of Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, we propose a simple interval sampling algorithm that can be used to provide qualitative insights into the behavior of the spectrum, significantly simplifying the design of simulation protocols. Our method allows us to easily visualize the complexity of the sign problem and to study the geometry of the sampling space. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides insights into the propagation mechanics of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic and offers potential solutions to mitigate their spread. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To further explore this concept, we conducted experiments using both stochastic gradient descent and Adam optimizer, with outcomes suggesting that model performance is indeed sensitive to loss function, and that certain loss functions can deliver results on par with the established mean squared error (MSE). Specifically, our research discovered that using mean absolute error (MAE) loss with MSE-based models can provide comparable performance. To facilitate replication and further investigation, we made all experiment codes and data publicly accessible. Additionally, we introduced an open question regarding the loss function in relation to model overfitting, and proposed several potential research directions. In the context of super-resolution, we explored loss function in the context of real-valued tasks, and proposed Slant MSE loss to improve performance. Our research aims to stimulate discussion within the community on loss functions, and invite experts to share their justifications for choosing specific loss functions. Moreover, we invite researchers to join us in investigating the complex relationships between loss functions, models, optimizers, and tasks at http://nnconvex.github.io/loss-ideas/, where we look forward to sharing replication codes, new findings, and integrating community contributions. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. The ability of the model to predict material behavior in different experimental setups is demonstrated through the simulation of large cyclic deformations with strain-induced crystallization. The theoretical model's capabilities are validated against available experimental data and compared to other similar models, which differs in assumptions and prediction of material behavior. Furthermore, the influence of key parameters on model predictions is examined through dimensional analysis. The potential of the model to account for various crystalline region properties, such as initial and final volume fraction, orientation, and degree of order, is also highlighted. The proposed model offers a comprehensive framework for modeling strain-induced crystallization in polymers and can effectively inform future experimental design. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our findings show that our method can effectively learn to prefer correct outcomes over wrong ones, even when the teacher's preference function is highly complex and diverse. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that high quality human feedback, labeled over the course of many comparisons, is not a prerequisite for successful learning. Instead, we find that even minimal human efforts can yield significant improvements if the sub-regional labels are tightly controlled to within 10% of the desired optimal policy. Furthermore, we explore various evaluation methods for assessing the quality of human provided labels and their impact on the learning agents. Ultimately, our findings suggest that true potential of human aided learning can be realized through the combination of advanced data visualization techniques and precise sub-regional labeling. In particular, we uncover that agents learn best from human labels that are tightly concentrated around high reward states. Additionally, we observe that the quality of human labels is highly variable and often correlates with the specific data visualization tools used. Consequently, we stress the significance of rigorous evaluation for both the learning agents and human labeling processes. Lastly, we highlight opportunities for future research to further optimize the interaction between humans and learning agents. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Additionally, we establish that the introduction of certain first-order axioms within set theory results in the appearance of additional model companions. This phenomenon leads to an infinite array of model companion theories of set theory, each corresponding to a distinct value of the infinite cardinal $\kappa$. Finally, we outline how this work relates to earlier research by Kayser and Friedman-Miller on model companions in set theory. This research has a significant implication, as it indicates that the concept of model companions is an effective tool for investigating various solutions to mathematical problems over set theory. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. For specific $k_n$ values, particularly when $k_n$ is sublinear in $n$ and equals $n^{\alpha}$ with $0 < \alpha < 1$, the asymptotic distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations can be determined more precisely, resulting in a $n^{1/\alpha}$-scaled beta distribution. Additionally, this work demonstrates the applicability of parking sequence theories to establish new bounds for last place estimates or absolute differences between uniform distribution functions on integers. These bounds can be tailored to yield specific $k_n$-dependent limits for the first $k_n$ locations. Finally, this work is concluded by presenting an intuitive analysis to illustrate the asymptotic behavior of $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$ through circular permutation central limit theorem approximations, although this is shown to not provide a rigorous proof due to the slow convergence rate. Lastly, this work is motivated by prior research into the relationship between uniform distribution, conditional random walk, and parking sequence, and concludes with potential avenues for further exploration into the properties of parking sequences.

In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We used a simple methodology to assess the sensitivity of our model to input variations and found that it was an effective indicator of performance on new, unseen data. We evaluated our approach using various datasets and settings, demonstrating its capability to handle complex loss functions and adapt to diverse model architectures. This code also enables users to develop custom loss functions and adapt existing ones. We also developed a sensitivity analysis toolkit, which is comprised of a simple model that can be used to generate synthetic data and evaluate the effectiveness of various methods in capturing the sensitivity of inputs. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
The code and data for our research are available online.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth. In this'sweet spot', sticking forces dominate the movement of particles, supplanting the dominance of gravity in this range. In a further extension of prior research, the temperature at which the surface energy drops by a factor of 5 is found to be around 400-700 K. In addition, we discovered that increasing temperatures above 1200 K causes the destruction of grains, as well as the dispersion of the elements that make up the grains, which marks the end of their life cycle. In addition, we discovered that even in our vacuum-based experiments, particles are susceptible to being broken down at high temperatures due to molecular recombination. Furthermore, despite being carried out in a vacuum, we observed the growth of particles in the size range of 100-700 um at temperatures of around 1200 K, which we believe occurred as a result of the consolidation of particles that were previously broken down at higher temperatures. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code for our research is available online at the specified link. Through our work, we hope to contribute to the development of more versatile and adaptable kernelized learning methods for robot skill learning. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. As an interesting side discovery, certain six-gluon amplitude functions in N=4 SYM theory have been found to be non-trivial even when all external gluons are directed towards the same rapidity direction, a previously unknown limit referred to as the ultra-relativistic limit (URR). As predicted, under URR, conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory exhibit cross ratios of 1. Moreover, despite being independent of rapidity ordering in URR, the two-gluon CEV itself cannot be factored into a product of two single-emission CEVs for any order of rapidity. As such, the CEV for two gluons with all positive helicities in URR represents a novel contribution that can be made in the context of the BFKL equation, with potential to impact NNLL accuracy calculations. As an interesting theoretical exercise, this newly identified limit could be further explored to determine its broader implications for theoretical understanding of six-gluon amplitude functions in N=4 SYM theory. As a practical application of this discovery, further research is also recommended to determine whether this newly identified URRC scenario can be realized in experimental settings via deep learning techniques, with possible detection through pattern recognition methods. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Lastly, we analyze the influence of Rashba coupling on the superconducting state's topological stability across the phase diagram.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We provide concrete examples and empirical evidence illustrating the price of serial dictatorship in various applications, including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. Lastly, we outline potential research paths for further investigation.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From a total of 4574 monitored asteroids, our analysis identified 
856 binary prospects, including 24 previously known binary asteroids. Among 
these discoveries, we uncovered 6 new wide binary asteroids, along with 6 
additional binary prospects requiring high-resolution imaging for clarification. 
In addition, our research facilitated the reclassified status of 6 asteroids, 
previously marked as single objects. The results of our analysis are available 
on the NASA Dwarf Planet Finder website, featuring detailed descriptions of our 
analysis techniques, findings, and relevant data. The discovery of additional 
wide binary asteroids is crucial to maintaining the stability of binary asteroids
and informing our understanding of asteroid masses. As such, follow-up high-
resolution observations are necessary to confirm or deny the binary status

of these six new wide binary asteroids, along with the validation of six 
previous binary asteroid findings, contributes significantly to the small total

spread function analysis, which is capable of detecting smaller components of

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in structural styles, isostatic equilibrium, and stratigraphic patterns observed in 3D seismic and well log data from the West African and Brazilian conjugate margins.  This research offers a new perspective on the development of the South Atlantic conjugate margins and contributes to the broader understanding of intraplate extension and passive margin evolution.  It also highlights the significance of analyzing deformation data from multiple locations along a margin to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of conjugate margins.  This approach is critical for accurately modeling the evolution of the margin and predicting hydrocarbon occurrences.  The methodology proposed in this study can be applied to other rift and passive margins around the world.  It provides a new framework for analyzing the complex history of conjugate margins and informs strategies for interpreting 3D seismic and well log data in exploration missions.  Furthermore, it highlights the value of multi-disciplinary approaches that integrate geological, geochemical, geophysical, and biochemical data to understand the evolution of conjugate margins and reveal their hidden history.  This study offers a range of tools to address such challenges and provides opportunities for cross-disciplinary research to uncover the mysterious past of conjugate margins. images.  Furthermore, our technique exhibits superiority over baseline methods 
utilizing traditional contrastive learning techniques.  The source code is

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that incorporating a Dopamine-like reinforcement learning mechanism enhances the DMD's overall performance. The success we experience lays the groundwork for investigating how natural language interactions are influenced by concepts like intentions, beliefs, and preferences in the context of role-playing games. Moreover, we provide a dataset of convolutions conversations based on D&D rules, along with a DMD that can be used in further research initiatives. As such, we hope to contribute to the development of more sophisticated AI-powered interactive systems that can be evaluated through the lens of role-playing games. We present our research within the context of the 2022 AI4CSE challenge, alongside an exhaustive report on our methodology, findings, and the DMD code is available at https://github.com/ghulamena/dmd. We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. The definitions of these functions are derived from the dijet momentum imbalanced in e+e- reactions, involving quark and antiquark spinning differently, which leads to an association with boomerang-like motion. Consequently, we can view these functions as boomerang functions. It is also shown that the boomerang functions are a parton version of parton spin alignment functions mentioned in the context of hadron production in ep and $\gamma$p reactions. Furthermore, we derive explicit connections between the boomerang functions and the Boer-Mulders function, as well as $h_\perp$ functions associated with dijet momentum imbalanced in ep and $\gamma$p reactions. Finally, we comment on possible experimental accessibility of these boomerang functions in the near future.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. By incorporating time-dependent analysis to the existing method, we are able to precisely determine the folding rates of proteins with shallow and deep knots - rates that indicate proteins with shallow knots fold approximately 5 times faster than proteins with deep knots. This research showcases the capability of using advanced topological models to analyze the geometry and folding processes of knotted proteins. We believe that this statistical approach, along with its modified version, can provide valuable insights into the complex relationships between protein knots and their folding processes. Moreover, we think that this method paves the way for further investigations into various protein knots. As such, we are presenting a comprehensive dataset that includes the comparison of proteins with trefoil knots and also a list of proteins that have been categorized into shallow and deep knots categories. This dataset is available for download as part of our source code, and we are making it available to biologists and physicists to facilitate the investigation of folding processes of proteins with trefoil knots. Specifically, we are launching three specific challenges to explore the relationships between protein knots and their folding processes. Challenge 1 focuses on identifying factors that influence protein knots, while Challenge 2 aims to develop predictions on folding processes of proteins with trefoil knots. Challenge 3, on the other hand, seeks to compare the folding rates of proteins with shallow and deep knots. We hope that this research, along with the associated dataset and challenges, will contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between protein knots and their folding processes. This knowledge, in turn, can inform the design of drugs and other therapeutic interventions targeted at these complex molecular structures. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Furthermore, we investigated the stress of existing assumptions on our findings and confirmed that EDE could account for as much as $0.19$ of the total energy density today. Additionally, we analyzed three different scenarios for varying EDE properties across different regions and discovered that our results are robust across all scenarios, paving the way for more precise EDE property measurements with enhanced data sets. Lastly, we explored the impact of EDE on other cosmological parameters and discovered that it could be responsible for as much as $0.25$ of the total tension in the Hubble constant. Overall, our analysis provided a statistical evaluation of EDE within the framework of $\Lambda$CDM and suggested various pathways for enhancing future investigations. Lastly, we are preparing to integrate EDE models directly into analytical initial conditions for perturbation theory, which will allow for more precise predictions on subtle features of large-scale structure and potentially reveal further evidence for or against EDE. This work is part of broader research aims that aim to integrate EDE models with new or revised cosmological data and shed light on the fundamental properties of EDE. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. Although the hypothesis remains an open problem in number theory, some of the proposed solutions could have implications for better understanding the anomalous NG theorem. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, we observe that these improvements translate to real-world applications, yielding a 2% enhancement in semantic similarity and a 10% improvement in textual classification when aided by a mediator. The code and data developed as part of this research are available for public access at https://github.com/google-research/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. A theoretical model indicated that strain from the epitaxial relationship can significantly strengthen the spin-orbit coupling in LaPtSb, locating it in the DFT calculations. This study's findings suggest that remote epitaxy can be a versatile method for generating strain in Heusler compounds. Conclusion: The ability to easily vary strain in remote epitaxy, combined with the capability to incorporate multiple elements, may provide a path towards discovering new compounds with desired properties. This could be especially important for compounds that cannot be made bulk epitaxially due to high lattice mismatch with available substrates. This study offers a foundation for a systematic exploration of remote epitaxy, its theoretical underpinnings, and its potential applications in the field of Heusler compounds. This, in turn, may provide a route to discovering new compounds with desired properties, offering a promising direction for the development of this field. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  Moreover, the technique proves particularly beneficial for GANs trained on datasets with limited annotation, showcasing its versatility as a complementary method for generating multi-label data.  The code and models developed as part of this research are available for public access on GitHub.  This technique is thought to offer a potential solution to various setting-related problems encountered when applying current multi-label setting techniques to single positive label data.  Future work is planned to explore the technique's applicability to other setting settings including negative samples and distribution manipulation. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Thus, we propose that hadronic radiation from black holes in the centers of galaxies and the Earth's galactic center could be the source of gamma-rays often observed from cosmic air showers, and suggest that this could also hold true for larger-scale cosmic phenomena.  In addition, we suggest that the majority of gamma-rays from nearby galaxies could be attributed to jet radiation rather than hadronic radiation, and that more precise theoretical models are needed to better comprehend the mechanisms behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies.  Lastly, we propose that the cause behind clumps of massive stars forming in the Milky Way could be attributed to the influence of magnetic fields shaped by the actions of black holes at the centers of stars. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. We implemented our methods on real-world data sets, demonstrating their effectiveness. The code is available for public use.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The proposed method's performance, along with other techniques, is evaluated and compared to establish its feasibility for point-of-care cardiac auscultation applications.  The study's findings can serve as a foundation for further research aimed at enhancing the diagnosis of heart conditions through improved analysis of cardiac auscultation sounds. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code, data, and experiments are available at https://github/qasper.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, researchers, policymakers, and scientists must collaborate closely to develop, analyze, and utilize these models in a way that reflects the complexities of the underlying biology and has meaningful implications for society. Ultimately, this collaboration is crucial for leveraging mathematical modeling to address the ongoing public health crisis.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adabatic case, we obtained a more complex inelastic rotationally resolved model. In the absence of spin-exchange, a much simpler effective model applies, closely related to the three-body problem studied by Wittmann et al. in 2011. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The advantages of this new architecture are demonstrated through the creation of a fully functional genome editor that operates directly with DNA storage at a base-level. The tools developed as part of this research are made freely available for use and further development through our DNA-storage repository at https://github.com/kuicp/dns. MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Experimental results show MAG-Net's high accuracy in tumor type classification and segmentation, demonstrating potential as a reliable, real-world brain tumor diagnosis system.  This model's potential as a practical brain tumor diagnosis system is also explored by predicting tumor locations on unseen images without the need for ground truth data, confirming its utility in supporting radiologists during tumor treatment planning.  The model's code is available on GitHub, and we look forward to it being utilized by other researchers in this field.  This study's outcomes contribute valuable insights to the development of more effective, efficient deep learning models for brain tumor diagnosis.  Future directions for improvement are also identified, and we present a comparison of our findings with those of comparable studies.
