Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this framework offers a way to learn the illuminant's spectral properties directly from raw images, without relying on pre-computed illuminant estimates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by recovering multiple object properties at once and learning illuminant spectra in a single image scenario. Additionally, we show that our learned spherical approximations can be applied across new scenes, showcasing their versatility. Unlike current learning-based renderers that are confined to trained scenes and often produce visually distorted shadows, our method's accuracy in shadow rendering serves as a significant strength. Furthermore, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art models and traditional optimization methods in various experiments, highlighting its efficiency and superior performance. All code and data are openly available at https://github.com/lingidriver/SparseShadows. With this work, we establish a new benchmark for high-definition shadow rendering and set a new standard for the field. A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. The proposed system has particular applications in the post-production industry, specifically in visual effects and video editing. However, it can also be adapted for other interlacing-related tasks. The code for this research has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Notably, our SVE model exhibits higher precision and efficiency than the PCA-DNN and SE models, suggesting that it represents a more effective solution for this problem. In addition, our methodology is adaptable to different river flows and can be applied to other similar partial differential equations. Ultimately, our research offers a novel approach to predicting flow velocities in rivers, combining efficient numerical solutions with probabilistic modeling of the riverbed profile. This has the potential to enhance the management of flood risks and contribute to the development of more effective numerical solutions for similar partial differential equations. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Findings reveal that the BDDC algorithm is highly effective, requiring only a small fraction of the total memory, and demonstrating strong scalability, with a near perfect linear growth in memory usage with increasing grid resolution. Moreover, the project is completed within a day using 512 processors, indicating that direct solution methods can be successfully applied to solve large-scale cardiac mechanics problems. Additionally, the research highlights the potential for further optimization, as modest improvements to the algebraic multigrid method would result in even faster solution times. Nevertheless, the current implementation allows for realistic visualizations and simulations of heart motion, and provides a framework for exploring how to incorporate feedback from direct solution methods into the larger simulation, and using direct solution methods as a tool for better understanding the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue. The project, conducted by cardiology and computer science students, facilitates interdisciplinary research and showcases the value of collaborative efforts in this field. The implementation of the BDDC algorithm is openly available for public use, providing a viable solution for solving similar large-scale systems in the medical community. The success of this research paves the way for further investigations into the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue, and makes feasible more comprehensive feasibility studies that can be completed within a day using high-performance computing resources. Ultimately, the project marks an important milestone in achieving faster solution times, more feasible scalability, and a deeper understanding of how to effectively utilize direct solution methods for complex cardiac mechanics problems. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, EBOS represents a universally applicable technique that can be incorporated into virtually any classifier, based on its simple design that leverages existing loss functions and classification decisions. As a result, we expect this to have a significant impact on areas like risk-sensitive learning and constructive neural network design. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/chacdev/EBOS.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The code and environment are available online at https://github.com/Mistral42/L2Explorer, and we invite the research community to join us in exploring this groundbreaking benchmark environment. The L2Explorer website is also accessible at https://l2explorer.github.io/. The L2Explorer framework is part of the DeepSafe benchmark suite, a comprehensive collection of evaluation environments designed to assess safety-critical lifelong learning models. The suite is initiated by DeepSafe and aims to facilitate collaborative experimentation among research institutions. The L2Explorer website includes detailed instructions and is the primary hub for further development and contribution. The L2Explorer code is based on the Unity ML-Agents toolkit. The L2Explorer environment is feature-rich, incorporating a variety of actionable objects that can be manipulated by the agent. The training and evaluation frameworks for L2Explorer are implemented using the TensorFlow framework. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Our findings indicate that SPADE of this type can provide a more efficient approach to achieving super-resolved imaging, likely utilizing less optical system complexity than other proposals. Moreover, our research offers a general framework for evaluating SPADE that can be applied to a wide range of entangled source scenarios. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This implies bulge growth is the primary driver of this behavioral shift. Therefore, to complete the transformation of galaxies into massive ellipticals with low specific star formation rates, additional processes such as major mergers are still required. These mergers would then facilitate further bulge growth and help shape the bulge's structural properties. Prior research has established a link between the mass of a galaxy's central bulge and its effective radius. To build upon this understanding, examining how the growth of bulges contributes to the mass-radius relation is essential. By studying how rates of star formation within different galactic components contribute to the mass-radius relation, a more comprehensive picture of galaxy evolution can also be developed. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The evaluation shows that, depending on the specific program and protocol in question, successful fence insertion may be accomplished in time proportions as low as $O(n)$ or as high as $O(n^3)$. Additionally, the total fence cost is proportional to the program size in some cases, while it becomes a fixed multiple of the program size in other instances. The demonstration of the protocol's safety, on the other hand, can be accomplished in a time proportionate to $O(n)$. The overall program verification process, including fence insertion, can result in time proportions ranging from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^4)$. The research presented here provides the foundation for further exploration of methods that determine optimal fence placement. The proposed framework and associated algorithm for fence optimization have been conceptually outlined, and the description of the counter-example driven fence insertion procedure is seen as the primary step for any feasible method. Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. This finding is corroborated by both Liapunov exponent and phase space density analyses. Notably, the quantum kernal's behavior resembles the classical Liapunov exponent in proximity to the ground state, despite differing on longer timescales. This phenomenon is further illustrated through timeseries simulations. It's observed that quantum trajectories display chaotic paths indistinguishable from their classical counterparts, utilizing time-series data. This suggests that quantum time-series data can serve as a basis for inferring classical chaos in similar systems. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Through this work, a initial step is taken towards leveraging X-ray imaging and advanced computer vision techniques to predict severe COVID-19 symptoms, while also exploring the extraction of clinical image characteristics from datasets with ICU admission labels. As a result, this work has far-reaching implications for the use of quantitative image analysis to extract meaningful features from datasets across various medical applications. As such, this approach may be adapted for additional purposes, such as developing early warning signs for patients at risk of lung pathology based on their imaging history. To this end, the code developed as part of this research is made publicly available, representing a comprehensive framework that is ready for use in other medical applications involving image analysis. Furthermore, this factorization of W into a monadic structure and a natural transformation from that structure to itself reveals a connection to the Kleiman-Bousfield functor structure. This paper develops the simplicial universal bundle functor W further, giving it in terms of a natural transformation of monads for example. Finally, this paper identifies necessary conditions for a monadic structure on the category of simplicial objects in a category to be induced by a universal bundle functor. It also discusses the implications of these conditions for combinatorial, finite Grothendieck constructions in algebraic geometry.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zeangit/Sabra-vrd. Our work provides an effective solution to the VRD false positive issue and offers actionable insights for future research in the field. Visualizing the understood interactions between objects is a natural extension of our basic framework, and we have one such implementation here: https://zeangit.github.io/Sabra-vrd-vis/. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The performance capabilities of the CAPP were further assessed by executing various search algorithms, including hash tables, sorted lists, and binary search, which showed the CAPP to be comparable to a high-speed CPU like the Intel Core i7-6700K. The integration of multiple CAPPs was also explored, showcasing how multiple content-addressable arrays could be combined to achieve greater performance and data management capabilities. The CAPP has significant potential as a versatile, high-performance hardware component capable of efficiently executing various algorithms, merging multiple content-addressable arrays, and providing a accessible interface for external programs via simple instructions. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. Our research provides a novel perspective on the evolution of galaxies at $\rm z\sim3$, involving a interplay between quenching, star-formation, galaxy construction, bulk construction, and the influence of streams that fuel the galaxies. This phenomenon indicates a transition from an 'inside-out' quenching pattern seen in higher redshift levels. This research is further backed by a statistical analysis of a larger galaxy population consisting of seven galaxies at $\rm z=2.91$, as part of the EAGLE advanced computer simulation. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero. These findings are achieved through the development of a new compactness criterion in the context of Strauss's theorem. The arguments we present also enable the verification of the least energy condition among these "bubbling solutions". The interconnections between "bubbling solutions" and the symmetry of "bubbling subsets" are explored in the final section of our paper. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure. Furthermore, we observe our approach succeeds where a method that failed previously did not, specifically with more complex function scenarios. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. Our study demonstrates that our quantum-inspired method not only achieves comparable performance to these methods but also adapts quickly to data shifts, surpassing them in many cases. Moreover, our algorithm's performance is scalable, stable, and easy to parallelize. The code is openly available for use at https://github.com/leodst/quantanomaly.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Conversely, we find that even the most recent case of In re Grand Jury does not alter our existing understanding set forth in the paper. Lastly, we propose an alternative approach based on the 'hinting problem' to further delimit the scope of compelled action, with an example illustration using the example of compelled decryption. Ultimately, we contend that any action that provides a hint to data access can be viewed through the lens of the hinting problem. Consequently, we propose that the government's ability to access data through compelled action is akin to the ability to obtain a hint from the respondent, which in turn can be obtained by having the respondent perform an action where the action's outcome is informed by the relevant data, even if the action itself is not directly aimed at accessing the data. With this in mind, we present several new conclusions about compelled actability, including that certain types of multi-party computation are susceptible to compelled actability, whereas certain types of hash functions are not. Additionally, we find that compelled actability is inherently resident in encryption, making it a 'base case' that is irrevocable. Lastly, we propose that any action which enables the government to obtain a hint that is no more informative than what the government already has, is effectively compelled action that yields 'effective nothing', which we contend aligns with the doctrine established in the case of Fisher v. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability. The paper also shows that well-known classes, such as planar graphs and finite-degree graph classes, have the new property. The research implies that the technique can be applied to fractionally-closed classes under binary valuations, such as those defined by the NP-completeness criterion of Givens and Schaefer. The paper also presents a new property called diagonalisability and proves it for some classes and against it for others. The research on this property may be an interest in itself. The paper's results imply that the standard method by Baker can be replaced by a simpler method for specific graph classes and it enables the application of the technique to fractional CSPs for classes where Baker's method worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The research was done by extending the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values but contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. With a mass of 1.47 ± 0.08 solar masses, KIC 9267654 is the most substantial candidate to exhibit a mixed internal rotation pattern among the currently observed giant stars. Furthermore, this star exhibits an unusual low-velocity amplitude in its core, as well as a slow and irregular stellar rotation curve in its outer layers. Through gravitational imaging, we were able to resolve the star's pulsation patterns and determine the core and outer layer rotation rates. The core of KIC 9267654 rotates at 103 ± 13 km/s, while its outer layers rotate at 183 ± 10 km/s. This distinct internal rotation pattern suggests that the star possesses a complex internal structure, and may have experienced a significant internal event such as the merger of a planetary companion. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, an evaluation of the system's ability to recognize false information on new events revealed a remarkable 10% improvement in the accuracy level. The study paves the way for the development of other applications such as detecting misinformation in video narratives. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This is in alignment with similar results seen in one-dimensional periodic Euler and Boussinesq equations. Notably, it is proven that the solution will develop a finite-scale blow-up within a critical time frame of $O(1)$, when the initial data is smooth, has minimal amplitude, and has a critical wavelength of $O(1)$ in the opposite direction. This is in accordance with classical conservation laws, where solutions typically remain smooth for an infinite duration when the initial data has a wavelength of $O(1)$ in the opposite direction. This distinct characteristic is showcased through both analytical and numerical means. It is also shown that the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time is not allevged by the non-local nature of the flow, as well as the fact that fractional decay has a subcritical impact on slowing down the formation of singularity. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Finally, we conduct numerical analyses to present results for M/M/1/1 and M/G/1/1 queues.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field. Additionally, distinct examples of the U_q(su(2)) algebra have been classified based on their representation properties and set-theoretic solution-derived counterparts, further revealing that all such algebras can be expressed as crossed products of dual subalgebras and their Finkelstein twists. A key contribution of this research is the introduction of a new classification system for set-theoretic solutions and its application to various quantum algebras, including the E8 algebra and its U_q(su(2)) counterpart. By providing specific examples and describing their inherent properties and relationships, this research paves the way for more in-depth analysis of the underlying mathematics involved. Lastly, this work highlights the potential for set-theoretic solutions to serve as a unifying framework that encompasses both set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions within the field of quantum algebra and Yang-Baxter equations.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Furthermore, a short circuit method is presented to generate GCA of any desired size using pairs. This construction is theoretically justified through a technical lemma. This research also includes a discussion on GCA properties, such as their relationship to partial four-weight codes and complete weight spectra. A few examples of GCA arrays are constructed and presented in their explicit form. This work is significant as it addresses a long-standing open question concerning the sizes of GCA quadruples. This research is complemented by a database containing all constructed GCA pairs and quadruples. This database is periodically updateable and accessible via a linked database, which is also provided within this paper. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Alongside this, we developed a method to analyze the inherent properties and variations of a system, giving rise to the concept of a'system operator', which enables the mapping of a system's structure and dynamics to its underlying architecture and neural network representation, respectively. Ultimately, our research offers a groundbreaking perspective on the inherent nature of complex systems and their actionable insights for enhancing generalization capabilities. Additionally, we hope this will spark interest in exploring other complex systems and dynamical processes. All code and data are available at https://github.com/hengleiwang/graph_neural_systems, offering a foundation for further research and generalization in this field. With this work, we are opening up new avenues for the scientific community to build upon our findings and investigate the complex interactions underlying these systems. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Moreover, our approach enables us to develop an analytical expression for the counts of certain divisibility conditions meeting specific criteria, which corresponds to the computation of specific homology modules over the integers. We further establish connections to various enumerative geometric problems and propose conjectures related to these calculations and their connections to the stable homotopy theory of sphere spectra. We also introduce a new combinatorial operation that extends the behavior of the div card function from elementary to compound partitions, and we explore its properties and implications. We support our findings with extensive numerical calculations and tables, offering a basis for further theoretical analysis. These results have significant implications for understanding the graded structure of homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory and could have related consequences for the theory of stable homotopy classes of maps between sphere spectra. Additionally, they provide a foundation for investigating other divisibility conditions governed by the properties of the Witt vector construction and its interactions with the Milnor Moore algebra. We anticipate that our method of combinatorial calculation of homology module counts will be applicable to a broad range of scenarios beyond the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra and encourage mathematicians to explore its potential for other contexts. We have made the underlying software tools publicly available for reference and further development. We plan to build upon this groundwork by combining these results with related computations derived from the periodicity theory of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra to establish more comprehensive statements of count calculations for various divisibility conditions. We also intend to employ these conclusions to tackle various enumerative geometric problems and investigate the consequent implications for the stable homotopy theory of sphere spectra. We look forward to contributing to a full extension of the Gregory-Kriegskorte theorem and exploring the potential applications of this theory to the study of map classes between sphere spectra. We are particularly interested in examining the interplay between the counts of divisibility conditions and the values of Kronecker coefficients, as well as investigating the connections between these computations and the structure of homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. This proposed protocol has an entanglement cost of $4$, which is optimal since any entanglement-assisted protocol would require at least this much entanglement to distinguish the same UPB. Similarly, in $3 \otimes 4 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol with entanglement cost of $4$ was proposed to locally distinguish one such UPB, which is also optimal. These proposed protocols improve previously known protocols and demonstrate the smallest possible entanglement cost required to locally distinguish these UPBs. This research therefore provides a connection between the properties of UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions, and suggesting that many minimal UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality. It also highlights the importance of multiple-party systems in studying strong quantum nonlocality, and proposes new entanglement-assisted local distinguishability tasks. It also introduces a new family of UPBs in $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$, and provides lower bounds on the entanglement cost required to locally distinguish these UPBs. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Ultimately, this method exhibits potential to maximize the efficiency of optical fiber usage in massive spectroscopic surveys. Conclusion: The proposed algorithm effectively coordinates astrobots in the SDSS-V by establishing a complete coordination framework, and its cooperative artificial force architecture achieves optimal convergence and safety. This method's capability to handle various scenarios, a challenging catalog-based test case, and rare instances of incompleteness prove its viability. The algorithm's performance is further enhanced by the target assignment strategies, and minor adjustments address issues with convergence. This method's potential to maximize optical fiber usage in massive spectroscopic surveys makes it a suitable approach. The algorithm's efficient trajectory generation and cooperative architecture also merit consideration for other coordinate-sensing applications. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a result, the producer thread's performance, reliant on the output of the detector, is similarly enhanced, achieving a tenfold increase in efficiency. Additionally, the optimisations and resulting improvements have been validated through multi-threaded program executions on top of the GP 2 runtime environment. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains. The article also delves into the complexities of nonlocal problems with irregular boundaries, discussing recent research and examining the relationship between boundary singularity and the nonlocal interaction parameter. The article concludes by highlighting open questions in this field. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. The source code is available for review and modification at https://github.com/ahmadouas/sun-360-stitching. The findings reported in this research have significant implications for the broader field of stitching images from rotating cameras. Further research is needed to explore applications for these approaches, particularly those involving non-vertical axis alignment and based on modern deep learning techniques. The project also highlights the potential uses of the Sun360 dataset, the first public dataset featuring panoramic images, for evaluating stitching techniques and analyzing scene understanding. Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. 
This expansion is valid across a specified range of parameters $s_1,s_2$ and 
includes a detailed analysis of the relevant zeros. 
Furthermore, applying this result to the functional equation of the Eisenstein series 
yields conclusions about the spectra of these representations $\Delta(\tau,m)$. 
This outcome is particularly notable as it provides a novel proof of Weyl law for $\Delta(\tau,m)$. 
Additionally, this proof can be adapted to apply to a broader category of square-integrable automorphic representations. 
For the case where $\tau$ is ramified, the proof can be further adapted to show that the invariant measure on the unit sphere in $GL(m,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ has a discrete spectrum with explicit, constant values. 
This result can be extended to a broader class of compact subsets within $GL(m,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. 
Finally, the application of this approach has yielded new insights into the geometry of Eisenstein series cancellations, 
leading to the derivation of nontrivial bounds on the cancellation depth in various scenarios. 
These results can be viewed as contributions to the broader framework introduced by Hoffstein and Kumar. 
Alongside these outcomes, this work introduces several novel formulas related to Eisenstein series and representation theory, 
along with a novel approach to combining representation theory and number theory. 
This combination of principles and results is set to facilitate further research into the interconnections between algebraic geometry, number theory, and representation theory. 
This work is intended to serve as a initial step in a broader investigation aimed at exploring the possibilities of using automorphic forms to solve linear and quadratic equations over numbers and functions over curves, 
and as such, it presents several challenges and open questions waiting to be addressed.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn appears to deplete the gas available for star formation, as we have previously shown in earlier works. As a result, a major merger can take several billion years to use up all the available gas. Nevertheless, our data also show that merger shocks can generate massive star formation regions and stimulate the formation of active supermassive blackholes, both within a similar time frame of 1-3 billion years. Therefore, we propose that merger shocks can essentially dictate the cosmological origin of active supermassive blackholes and their relationships with super-solar abundance patterns seen in certain population of ultra metal poor stars in our galaxy today. These stars were likely born during the early stages of the galaxy's merger history that shaped our galaxy. Ultimately, our study provides a framework for studying active galactic nuclei and the interaction of galaxy mergers, a research perspective that will be informed by upcoming radio and millimeter wavelength facilities such as ALMA, NOEMA, and EVGA, as well as optical and near infrared facilities such as NOAO/NOIR-1, SOAR, and TNG. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our experiment employs successive reductions in the number of classes to classify snow, fog, rain, snow-or-fog, and rain-or-fog, demonstrating accurate results across all scenarios. 
Notably, this is the first study to tackle the classification of multiple weather conditions simultaneously. 
Our proposed method provides multiple class balancing techniques and showcases the effectiveness of data augmentation with super-pixel masks. 
The code and dataset are available online at this link https://github.com/ashfjk/Multi-Weather-Recognition. 
Our approach achieves outstanding performance and lays the groundwork for further research into multi-class weather recognition. 
In the long run, this could enable advanced driver-assistance systems to detect changing weather conditions more effectively. 
Ultimately, this has the potential to contribute to improved traffic flow and driver behavior.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Additionally, comparisons with other efficient models revealed the DPCRN's superior performance. The DPCRN model's simplicity and effectiveness make it a viable approach for speech separation applications. Furthermore, code and model repositories are available online for reference.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density. Further research aims to enhance the method's precision and extend it to other observables. This approach may provide a more objective method for identifying glueball states and could be applicable to other observables. This approach could be a crucial step in determining the spectrum of lattice QCD through spectral functions rather than relying on theoretical interpretations of spectral density or state-by-state studies. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. An
interesting observation emerged when we adapted this model to analyze the sentiment ex-
pressed not just towards specific users but also towards particular topics. Our findings
indicated that the topics generated by latent Dirichlet allocation can be used to modify the
model's perception of the sentiment expressed towards them. Finally, we presented a method
to track the evolution of public sentiment regarding these topics over time. We explored
these topics further by applying our proposed method to analyze the sentiment expressed
towards them in relation to the election campaigns of Indian prime ministers. We also
examined the sentiment expressed towards these topics in daily tweets. In conclusion, we
believe that our approach offers a useful framework for monitoring public sentiment ex-
pressed on Twitter. Alongside the code and dataset, we have an accompanying article
published in the Journal of Big Data available at reference [1].

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study demonstrates that the shadow radius can serve as an therapeutic probe for understanding thermodynamic phase transitions in black holes. Ultimately, we propose that this shadow radius approach be further explored in relation to other phase transitions in black holes, including those involving vector fields and 5-dimensional black holes. Lastly, we consider the practical feasibility of measuring this shadow radius through high-energy particle experiments, specifically the Future Electron-Positron Collider, which could provide a direct theoretical connection to such experiments. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Additionally, we illustrate practical applications of this concept through examples involving multimode systems and suggesting that this approach can be extended to other continuous-variable systems. This research brings forward a new vision where the study of light states transitions from looking at the state itself to understanding the physical phenomena it represents, by observing the effects these states have on detecting systems, such as collecting an optical tomogram. This new perspective is backed by mathematical proofs and illustrated with entanglement detection, demonstrating that entanglement exists by analyzing changes in an optical tomogram. This research also presents an alternative method for investigating light state dynamics, replacing conventional approaches that focus on state transitions themselves, replacing them with the study of how detecting systems, such as collecting an optical tomogram, monitor the effects of these states. This new perspective is backed by mathematical proofs and illustrated with state transition scenarios involving the von Neumann entropy of an optical tomogram. This research also presents an alternative method for investigating light state dynamics, replacing conventional approaches that focus on state transitions themselves, backing this new perspective with mathematical proofs and illustrating it with state transition scenarios involving the von Neumann entropy of an optical tomogram. This new perspective is also valid for detecting systems that have interactions with the environment, such as electromagnetic fields that interact with cavity modes, also known as open systems, and is illustrated with quantum synchronization in a system composed of two cavities.
