Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and data generated by our approaches are made publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/role-constrained-dialogue.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that certain insect growth regulators can reduce the disease risk and increase yields and profit without significantly increasing production costs. Furthermore, the quantile regression model helped allocate variable costs according to disease pressure levels. This approach provides a statistical solution to the efficacy evaluation problem and can be applied to other similar scenarios involving disease management. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential for this model to become a decision-support tool, helping farmers make informed decisions about pesticide applications under uncertain disease pressure conditions. This, in turn, could contribute to the sustainable use of pesticides. Finally, we suggest future directions for incorporating biological control methods into this framework. This research has the potential to become a foundation for data-driven decision-support systems aimed at optimizing pesticide applications in various agricultural contexts. By integrating biological and environmental data, such systems could further enhance the efficacy of pesticide use. Ultimately, we propose that this type of framework should be part of a larger initiative aimed at developing data-driven decision-support tools for sustainable agriculture practices. This would not only benefit farmers but also contribute to the meaningful use of big data in agriculture, in turn, informing best practices for the effective integration of machine learning methods in this field. require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the proposed model's performance with natively
captured data surpasses it with artificially generated data. The proposed
algorithm's effectiveness is further highlighted by a notable reduction in bandwdith
requirements for seamless video streaming. The proposed system's efficacy is
demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation of multiple scenarios, leading to
encouraging outcomes. The proposed system's code is openly available for use at
https://github.com/sonndt/vpp-s4k. The proposed system's potential to stream
360-degree videos with optimal viewport prediction was validated with real-world
data and subsequently incorporated into the 360DegreePlayer, a cutting-edge
video streaming application. The application, whose code is openly available

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Our proposed method provides a significant enhancement to existing tensor network algorithms, given its ability to overcome previous limitations in approximating the thermal behavior of systems developed from strongly interacting, biased photons in optical lattices. This development also paves the way for a full theoretical analysis of quench scenarios in these systems, enabling the identification of distinctive signatures that could be tested experimentally. We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. Along the way, we create a set of tools that can be used for surface analysis, including a function to compute the inner and outer approximations of a surface, as well as a method for determining whether a given surface contains a specified point. These tools are then employed in a procedure to find surfaces that satisfy specific conditions in relation to given parameters. We also illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to various problems related to the study of line segments. In particular, we use our surface-based approach to address concerns typically resolved by linear segmentwise analysis. We also demonstrate the benefits of our approach by solving a set of critical problems that arise in the context of our research. To further expand our theory, we investigate the properties of surfaces that can be expressed as the sum of two given surfaces, and we also consider the behavior of surfaces that result from the composition of two given surfaces. We also establish a relationship between the surfaces that have the same tangent direction at a specific point, as well as the surfaces that have the same tangent direction everywhere. We also discuss various other properties and open questions related to our research. We support our theoretical findings with concrete examples and illustrations. We also provide a surface library that includes a range of high-order smooth surfaces, as well as a sample implementation of our algorithm. We also present several critical problems that we solved using our approach. We hope that our work will inspire further research and development of our theory and its applications. In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. This involves the discovery that certain potentials satisfy a modified anisotropic Berndt-Riemer equation, which can be solved using a technique introduced in the reference provided. This technique involves an anisotropic approach to the method of sub and super solutions. This advancement enables the creation of sub and super solutions for equations of the nonlinear type encountered in the context of anisotropic Minkowski inequality. As a result, we obtain the minimum value of the energy functional associated with these equations, which includes both linear and nonlinear equations. This allows us to establish the validity of inequalities, including sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and anisotropic Willmore inequality. This research provides a foundation for further investigation into nonlinear potential theory and geometric analysis. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. Unfortunately, this approach still leaves significant portions of relevant data unusable. This issue highlights the importance of developing strategies to handle such events, either by reducing the satellite's vulnerability to solar flares, identifying earlier indicators to prevent data from the onset of a glitch, or implementing alternative data analysis methods that can better handle the effects of glitches. Ultimately, finding alternative strategies will be crucial for creating more precise tests of the weak equivalence principle in future space experiments. This study presents various approaches to mitigating the gluechs' impact on the principle test, including incorporating machine learning algorithms and analyzing the events themselves. While there are challenges to be addressed, the field of gravity physics stands to benefit significantly from the development of more sophisticated satellite platforms capable of withstanding glitches once. This study uses all available data from the Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle, encompassing approximately 45,000 orbits around the Earth, to investigate the effect of glitches on the principle test. The most significant violations of the principle occurred at frequencies related to the satellite's movement, specifically its orbital and rotational cycles. The structure of the glitches themselves, while relatively short-lived, had a substantial impact on the principle test result. The key factor influencing the effect glitches have on the principle test is the duration of the acceleration fluctuation, with larger glitches causing greater violations, regardless of their frequency. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. These results are particularly relevant to the behavior of cells during chemotherapy treatments.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete. Specifically, we prove a graph G has a 2-strong shortest path cover if and only if it is 2-link forest-free, and provide an NP-certification for this condition. Additionally, we provide a 2-hops cover time complexity of O(n^2 * m^n), where n is the number of vertices and m is the number of states in the Turing machine that determines forest-freeness. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between k-hops strong shortest path covers and k-hops forest-free covers, and conclude that determining the minimum k-hops cover is NP-complete even for weighted graphs. Finally, we provide lower bounds on the ratio of k-hops forest-free covers to k-hops strong shortest path covers, and determine the minimum ratio for certain graphs, including trees and random graphs. Last, we pose several open questions related to k-hops strong shortest path covers.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Additionally, we establish the recurrence or transience threshold for the frog model within a broader class of power-law graded graphs. Furthermore, we examine the exotic version of the model, revealing that it mimics the standard model's behavior at the same critical point. Our findings are accompanied by rigorous proofs and intuitive analyses, providing greater insight into the model's dynamics. Moreover, our research is supplemented by computations that validate the critical point's accuracy through various simulations. Ultimately, our study identifies the pivotal role that the tree's degree or underlying graph structure plays in determining the model's transient or recurrent behavior. This understanding is made possible by deriving lower bounds for the model's harmonic measure, which is critically linked to the existence of transient behavior. Lastly, we explore implications of our results for the model's dynamics and discuss potential directions for further research. These considerations are particularly relevant in the context of higher degrees and more complex graph structures.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Our research introduces a novel application of decision boundary analysis in knowledge distillation and offers efficient solutions for black-box distillation. This could have broader implications for understanding and manipulating complex neural networks. This study's unique contribution is recognized by the award it received at the 14th Asian Conference on Machine Learning 2022. This paper has also been accepted for publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. The accepted version is available at: https://jmlr.org/submissions/jmlr2022/wang_2022.html. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The resulting model is evaluated against a variety of observational limits including those from recoils experiments, and the associated implications for the model are found to be significant enough to influence the interpretation of upcoming dark matter experiments. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, we demonstrate real-world applications featuring the EG-CNN module in medical image processing. The open-source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yunusajith/Edge-Gated-Convolutional-Neural-Networks.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we identified potential issues with the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols in certain deployment scenarios. Our approach can be applied to any NoSQL database that supports multi-user transactions and verifies the consistency guarantees provided by its transaction protocol. We also established a baseline for evaluating the consistency guarantees provided by distributed transaction protocols. Our work is relevant to researchers and developers who seek to analyze and evaluate the consistency guarantees provided by database transaction protocols. Our implementation of the MongoDB transaction protocols, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, is available under the MIT license, and can be used as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of distributed database systems. For future work, we suggest extending this approach to evaluate the consistency guarantees provided by distributed transaction protocols in general. Additionally, we propose using this approach to analyze and evaluate other distributed storage systems. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the adverse impact of intrinsic bias on models when trained on biased datasets, even when data augmentation is employed.  Our research offers a initial step towards tackling the challenging problem of bias detection in medical image datasets. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Moreover, the proposed methodology achieves superior performance compared to other domain adaptation methods in a real-world live data scenario, with results amounting to a 28% enhancement. The successful adaptation of models to new domains has far-reaching implications for various applications, encompassing speech sentiment analysis and emotion recognition in real-world settings, and could also have a complementary effect with other techniques that rely on domain knowledge. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, our results demonstrate that higher pressure can recover the magnetic order at low temperatures despite initial loss, with further research needed to comprehend this effect.  Moreover, our analysis of dielectric measurements discloses the progression of dielectric loss peaks in BFTO under high pressure, with increasing pressure causing these peaks to shift towards higher temperatures.  We attribute these observations to competing energy factors related to structural adaptation, magnetic order and dielectric behavior, with pressure providing an additional stimulus for these changes.  We propose that BFTO under high pressure conditions makes it an appropriate material for the study of magnetic phase transitions in compound perovskites.  We also suggest that BFTO may provide a suitable framework for understanding the interactions between structure, chemistry, and physical properties in other materials experiencing multiple phase transitions with varying energy scales.  We highlight the potential for combining structural, chemical and physical analysis with theoretical modeling to understand the underlying principles governing the effects of high pressure on materials with complex structures, with multiple phases and competing energy factors.  We believe that BFTO, due to its unique five-layer structure and multiple phase transitions, provides a suitable opportunity for such a comprehensive study.  We anticipate that the unique features of BFTO, a compound with a complex structure experiencing multiple phase transitions, will make it an appropriate material for understanding the effects of high pressure on the interplay between structure, chemistry, and physical properties. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. This edge could be seen as marking the beginning of a new universe forming within the shock wave. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The 2015 data, incorporating 15 distinct collision patterns and around 200 kNOTS scenarios, showed strong agreement between predicted and observed data and marked a significant advancement in understanding long-range effects and beam behavior at the LHC. Building on this success, emittance scans will continue to play a crucial role in monitoring beam performance and validating lattice design for future upgrades to the LHC, specifically with regards to the Large Hadron Collider Upgrade Phase 2 and 3. Furthermore, the experience gained with emittance scans has informed the development of optimized beam filling schemes and prognosis tools for beam operation at the LHC. This report reviews the development and implementation of emittance scans, examining their measurements and their implications for LHC performance, in addition to discussing their influence on other projects, such as future colliders and energy recovery linacs. The report also outlines proposals for enhanced scanning strategies and new measurements that could be implemented with minimal additional resources, set against a backdrop of anticipated LHC performance improvements and the potential for them to impact the need for emittance scans. The report also includes the initial findings of applying the TRAIN code to the Future e+ e- Colliders, specifically the 24 GeV Advanced Super Conducting Proton-Proton Collider and the 250 GeV Future e+ e- Collider, as well as discussions on the potential for emittance scans to be utilized in other particle physics experiments. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes elements that can be easily extended by the community via its simple and modular design. The package has already been utilized in developments related to the Case-Dark Energy Trial (C-D4) experiment, one of the current stage-4 experiments. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Furthermore, our technique showcases superior robustness and adaptability in low-data scenarios and outperforms top competing methods by a significant 12% in average F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.64) for a extensive real-world dataset. The code is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghruyaa/MD-CSDNetwork.

Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Furthermore, with the source phase fixed, we found that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security when using single weak coherent states, and that the system requires the use of multi-weak coherent states to maintain security. Lastly, our research reveals that the proposed attack's success depends critically on the specific QKD system parameters, and that certain system parameters can provide a level of security against this attack, albeit possibly insecure against other hacking strategies. Our study provides a crucial basis for the development of genuinely secure QKD systems. Our simulations are executed using QWKD, a widely used Python QKD simulator. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our methods on network scalability and interoperability with other networks, emphasizing the importance of open, standardized, and modular approaches for achieving optimal performance in this context. Finally, we outline key research challenges and potential areas for further exploration in this field.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it demonstrates that metric spaces with angle functions can be viewed as a subset of the structure of semi-metric spaces with angle functions. This framework also facilitates the identification of additional properties that are inherent to the structure of Euclidean spaces. As such, it may be utilized as a framework for examining the concept of geometry in the context of spaces with angle functions. This article also introduces the notion of "Euclidean-like" spaces, which it defines as spaces that combine distance preservation with angle function preservation. This definition is applied in a discussion of spaces with angle functions that are focused on the structure of Euclidean spaces, specifically in the context of Menger's second problem. The discussion reveals that "Euclidean-like" spaces are equivalent to the composition spaces of metric spaces with angle functions, which are focused on the structure of Euclidean spaces. This article also delves into an examination of the relationship between spaces with angle functions and their focus spaces, which are spaces that have been composed from themselves to obtain a new space. In this examination, it is discovered that focus spaces can be viewed as a subset of "Euclidean-like" spaces. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, we present non-trivial examples of bounds for specific ratios of minima in quadratic, cubic, and quartic number fields. Moreover, we describe a method for counting the number of embeddings of a number field within a higher-degree field and apply this count to derive relationships between its minima. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture relating the structure of inequalities to the geometry of the Galois orbit of an order and offer evidence for this conjecture through computer simulations. This work is a significant expansion of previous research, offering a comprehensive examination of the complex interplay between the geometric structure of number fields and the norms of their orders. It is also a crucial step towards resolving open problems in geometry and algebraic number theory.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Our research extends the application of DRO models in real-world scenarios with significant data sets, encompassing image classification using large datasets like CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. DR-DSGD's code is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our research reveals the methods used by Forsage's developers to prevent detection and counter threats to the scheme, as well as the consequences they had for users and the scheme's participants. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings for the development of blockchain-based pyramid schemes and the challenges faced by participants in evaluating the credibility of developer claims about their smart contracts. Our investigation into Forsage lays the groundwork for a deeper research into blockchain-based pyramid schemes and facilitates an examination of the underlying mechanisms driving success in such schemes. Ultimately, our study illuminates the unseen aspects of these schemes through the example of Forsage, shedding light on participants' motivations, transaction dynamics, and the intricate workings of these types of agreements. Due to the unique visibility of Forsage's transactions, enabled by its blockchain foundation, it is an ideal subject for an in-depth analysis of pyramid schemes. It is hoped that this research will lay the groundwork for a comprehensive examination of Forsage's place within the broader context of pyramid schemes across different cultures and time periods. Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. The implemented methodology demonstrated success, and future directions for related studies are also outlined. Additionally, an online dashboard was created to visualize and explore the insights derived from the Twitter data, demonstrating the potential of social media data to inform public opinion and guide crisis communication strategies. This research was presented at the 2021 IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence for Modern Mobility Services, where an accompanying demo was awarded second place. The developed dashboard is now an open-source contribution for the research community. The data collected and analysis results have been shared with relevant stakeholders, including emergency management officials and Izmir city authorities. The methods employed in this study could be applied to examine other crises or events in Turkey or internationally. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. Additionally, we incorporated diversity factors into our predictions, and the associated code is available for use or adaptation with similar location data from broadcast videos of football matches.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of artificial networks suitable for testing and validating measurement methods. The full source code is available for public use, facilitating comparative studies between future method developments. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. These characteristics make the algorithm versatile and effective across a wide range of applications, including the distribution of digital certificates in large, distributed systems and the estimation of network size in peer-to-peer networks. The algorithm's design is built around a probabilistic technique called the "low-degree verification" protocol, and the algorithm can be employed in a broader context as well. The same algorithm enables a key application - namely, the compilation of a reliable node list in the network. The reliability of the algorithm is ensured by the verification of a key property by big players in the network, which in turn enables the proper functioning of the algorithm despite the presence of malicious nodes. The algorithm's characteristics make it an useful tool in the context of peer-to-peer networks, particularly in the construction of reliable lists of nodes in large networks. The paper also presents the algorithm's design, its properties, and the techniques used to enhance its performance, as well as the results obtained from conducting numerous simulations. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated by the significant improvement it yields over earlier proposals proposed in the state of the art, and the robustness of the algorithm is proven through an analysis of its behavior in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes. The paper concludes by highlighting the algorithm's numerous applications, its implications for the construction of reliable lists of nodes in large networks, and its potential uses in peer-to-peer networks. This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
The research uses data from the Texas A&M Smart Mobility Tunnel but analyzes
queue lengths during the red phase. The method's signal period independence is
demonstrated through estimation and variation analysis in independent data sets. 
The proposed approach is part of a larger traffic management concept that
estimates queue conditions and provides real-time feedback to optimize phase switching. 
Initial results show potential for reducing wait times and minimizing queue lengths. 
The method's simplicity makes it suitable for low-cost, easy-to-deploy hardware. 
The research uses a single lane but lays the groundwork for multi-lane applications.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. This breakthrough provides a crucial performance enhancement for future simulations of numerical relativity with fundamental fields. This method is currently employed in ongoing research involving the study of gravitational waves in the early universe. This project was carried out with computational resources provided by the University of Oulu and the Partnership for Advanced Computing in Europe (PRACE), leading to a publication in Physical Review D. This paper highlights the advantages of this new approach, the effectiveness of the multigrid solver, and the characteristics of the solutions obtained for various scenarios. It also sets the stage for further investigations into the role of spacetime singularities in generating gravitational waves in the early universe. This project is part of a broader project to explore the properties of gravitational waves taught by Juan Antonio del Pino. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate notable anomalies in the thermal gradient profile and provide a theoretical basis for the observed anomalous Nernst effect, both of which can be understood in relation to the material's crystal structure and electronic properties. Notably, our study indicates that the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is dominated by anti-ferromagnetic order and electron skewness, exhibiting a primary contribution from scattering by phonons and a lesser but notable influence from scattering by electrons, particularly at higher temperatures. Our research provides a theoretical framework for the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials and sets a new standard for accurate measurement of this phenomenon. Moreover, our results can be applied to a broader class of antiferromagnetic materials. Additionally, we propose that these materials are ideal for developing thermal Hall biosensors capable of distinguishing between biomolecule-capped gold nanoparticles of different sizes. Finally, we anticipate that our study will contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable measurement techniques for the anomalous Nernst effect in complex magnetic materials. Moreover, we suggest combining these materials with ferromagnetic materials to develop more effective and adaptable magnetic sensors. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, our findings also enable the development of new tests for evaluating a quantum annealer's competence and efficiency in managing complex phenomena affecting these systems.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. The writing draws on previously overlooked archival materials to offer a fresh perspective on the lab's past. The author, a professional astronomer, draws on his own experience to provide an objective evaluation of the developments that shaped the lab's history during this period. The study is completed with an assessment of how the successes and setbacks of the lab during this period influenced its position in the broader context of Dutch astronomy. The writing is informed by the author's own participation in the discussions that led to the establishment of the AAV-MBA, the Dutch national astronomy foundation. The study is concluded with suggestions on how to foster the growth of the foundation in the face of declining fundamental research funding in the Netherlands. We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications. Additionally, we propose that true collective wisdom arises when individual intellect is aligned with its goals. Human examples, particularly highlighting the benefits of synchronized thinking in meditation and the drawbacks of individual intellect in scientific competition, further illustrate our findings. Lastly, we suggest that a focus on internal knowledge may lead to greater collective progress than a focus on external knowledge.

Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Alongside these findings, we establish the connection between the graph $\Gamma$ and the group's action on the tree, which allows us to direct the discussion towards future research possibilities. These results are achieved without relying on the classification of finite simple groups.

Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Alongside outstanding performance, DECENNT-generated graphs provide actionable insights for researchers and experts in various domains. The code for DECENNT is now available on GitHub.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. In particular, we demonstrate the NN's effectiveness in machine learning, specifically for low-density separation and embedded multi-task learning. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets, showcasing a 10-30% improvement in test accuracy and up to 3 times faster training compared to popular deep learning frameworks. The Nested Neumann method is open-source and available on GitHub. In addition to its practical utility, the method offers a novel theoretical contribution to approximate matrix inversion. In conclusion, the NN algorithm represents a powerful fast approximate iterative method for matrix inversion, capable of reducing computational resources, Rash dependencies, and latency while enhancing convergence and accuracy. The method has far-reaching implications for linear algorithms operating on large datasets due to its minimal additional cost per iteration. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of topological Anderson phases in device demonstrations, such as neutral light switches and chiral transport.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrated that off-the-shelf learning algorithms can yield top-performing decoders for specific error scenarios, even in scenarios with prolonged decoding times and extended physical qubit loss. Additionally, we show that these learned decoders can be adapted through transfer learning to different noise models, eliminating the need for retuning the decoder in response to changes in error dynamics. As a bonus, we developed a decoder that can learn from a single data set corresponding to a specific noise model, to which a small amount of faulty data can be added by reinforcing errors. We anticipate that this novel approach to decoding will spur the development of complex quantum systems, enabling the study of system dynamics and performance evaluation in the presence of qubit loss. Furthermore, we anticipate that this approach will also inspire the development of learning algorithms for other critical quantum processing tools, such as quantum error correction hardware. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. However, the analysis of moderator effects revealed that the Scrum method's influence on project success is dependent on other factors, including company culture, team composition, and project characteristics. Our research provides actionable recommendations for project managers to adapt Scrum in distributed teams and ensure the basic needs of their remote workers are met. Ultimately, our study offers a foundation for further exploration into the intersection of home working, Scrum, and project success. By addressing the challenges associated with distributed Scrum, our findings can be applied to various fields that rely on software development, including those affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, this research can serve as a starting point for investigating the adoption of other Agile methodologies in remote working contexts. As such, it is relevant to field studies and invites further empirical validation from practitioners who have experienced the challenges of collaborating on Scrum projects from home. As the world adapts to new hybrid ways of working post-pandemic, this research provides valuable insights for overcoming the difficulties associated with distributed Scrum and achieving project success. As many companies are transitioning to a hybrid working model, combining home and office working, the findings of this study are highly relevant and can serve as a starting point for investigating the challenges associated with collaborating on Scrum projects in this new context. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the connection between the LCST and the Fourier Transform, and establishes the existence of the inverse Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform. Furthermore, inequality bounds for the LCST are derived, including a Hadamard inequality and a norm inequality, and the paper also analyzes the relationship between the LCST and the stockwell transform. The research is conducted within the context of function spaces that are defined by the LCST. The paper also provides an example of an infinitely differentiable function that is not analytic, using the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. As such, this study does not provide characterizations for extrema in those situations. As an added aspect, this research presents an alternative, straightforward proof for establishing extremal gain characterizations in its own right. As one such benefit, it provides an approach that is independent of previous methods that relied heavily on interference alignments. As a distinct finding, an analysis on the extremal gain of optimal over binary power control in specific $K^{2}$-shaped networks was conducted, revealing the gain itself is actually the extremal gain itself, amounting to nothing more than the additional gain itself, with it being proportionate to $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step algorithm offers a significant improvement for accurate simulations of complex sediment transport. Additionally, we found that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, and recommend using the largest feasible collision time steps if bias is acceptable. However, for accurate simulations of particle collisions, our multiple-time-step algorithm becomes necessary. Furthermore, we suggest that future researchers consider using highly efficient numerical methods such as the simplified direct numerical integration method for particle collisions. Our algorithm is highly efficient and has no coding complexity compared to the standard method, and we are confident that it will significantly enhance the simulation of complex sediment transport and other multiphase flows.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. Additionally, we derive the highest power of $2$ that can be achieved through this factorization, determining it to be $\frac{4-n}{3}$, and further determine that $n$ can range between $1$ and $3$ to produce valid pairs $(a,b)$. We also outline a method for generating pairs under a specific factorization condition, and discuss the relationship between the number of such pairs and the corresponding factorization exponent. Lastly, we propose a conjecture related to the number of pairs (a, b) for a given factorization exponent n, and offer supporting evidence.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached 70% of the desired height in a single hop. However, larger foot sizes resulted in decreased efficiency due to the buildup of granular material underneath. To move forward, we propose integrating this force-controlled one-legged hop to a higher-level balance control system to enable the robot to navigate complex deformable terrain. This approach is supported by research indicating that local stability on soft ground is determined by a limited set of critical frequencies, providing a plausible framework for its implementation. This work paves the way for the development of a deformable terrain-aware robot by integrating a one-legged hop into a higher-level balance control system. This system is anticipated to facilitate the efficient and stable navigation of complex ground conditions.
