This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our study also compares the effects of wave surface curvature and vorticity on waves, demonstrating that while both influence stability, the primary driver of instability is the direction and intensity of the shear flow itself. Furthermore, we observed that highly nonlinear waves exhibit a behavior consistent with that of a rigid body rotation in classical dynamics, and that the water's surface elevation becomes irregular in the presence of strong vorticity. Lastly, we explored the equation's capabilities in modeling long-wave propagation, revealing that it accurately replicates the Euler equations' behavior in that context. Our research paves the way for a deeper investigation of the water's surface elevation's irregular patterns through the development of new numerical methods. By examining the equation's conserved properties, we are also prepared to analyze the role of dissipation in this scenario. Ultimately, our study provides a foundational framework for understanding the effects of nonzero constant vorticity on nonlinear surface gravity waves and lays the groundwork for future exploration of this phenomenon. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Furthermore, an increase in navigation speed was achieved by applying a layering strategy to the robot's movement, reducing traversal time by approximately 20%. Additionally, the system's ability to detect and respond to changes in the indoor environment was demonstrated through a moving robot experiment. Powered by a USB port, the sonar sensor module operates independently from the main robot computer, eliminating data interference and allowing for the simultaneous use of the sonar sensor module in other applications. This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our solutions with numerical examples. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Moreover, we find that interacting through dialogues poses unique challenges which cannot be fully mitigated by simply relying on the isolation of individual utterances. Ultimately, our innovative evaluation method and energetic discussions at the 2020 Dialog System Technology Challenge showcase the value of neural language models in guiding the annotation of dialog data and inform future directions in this area. The associated code and data sets are publicly accessible online.

Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to closed unions. Contrary to this hypothesis, we demonstrate that such conditions are not finite union-closed over limited scenarios. To disprove this hypothesis, we define a new set of bi-positional winning conditions known as 'energy conditions,' specifically tailored for totally ordered groups. Furthermore, we present an instance of two conditions within this new set whose union is not positionally significant. Building upon this finding, we theorize that any condition with this independence property shares similarities with energy conditions, especially those defined on totally ordered groups over cyclical sequences. Lastly, we formulate the 'Energy Condition Hypothesis,' stating that such conditions must possess a substructure analogous to that of additive congruences, and we speculate that this hypothesis is applicable across various game theoretic contexts. We also establish that certain instances of energy conditions with specific properties can be non-prefix-independent. Additionally, we present an example of a condition that is neither finite union-closed nor totally dependent on prefixes or suffixes. We conclude by outlining potential avenues for further research in this field.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. An individual analysis of the standard and asynchronous variables shows that the magnetic field strength in asynchronous polars can be genuinely harder, more intense, and less weak. This distinction further highlights the unique features of magnetic field radiation accretion in asynchronous polars, necessitating more in-depth study of this rare CV subcategory. This work is based on a thesis previously submitted by the author to the University of Southampton.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our evaluation will involve two different mesh configurations, 'fine' and 'coarse', with respect to the method's ability to achieve comparable error levels using significantly reduced degrees of freedom. To further understand the implications of using these reduction methods with different solving approaches, we'll compare their computational times and accuracy for both mesh configurations. Additionally, we'll consider the potential for parallelization strategies, including solving for different spatial degrees of freedom on multiple CPUs, and discuss the related challenges and advantages. Through our investigation, we aim to provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating RB solutions in the context of FSI, and to facilitate a better understanding of how to effectively employ RB in conjunction with FSI methods, especially in relation to the use of monolithic or partitioned approaches. This project is conducted within the context of the MODHUM project, focused on modeling cardiac electrophysiology, and utilizes the FEniCS framework for finite element method implementations. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This proposal suggests using atomic interferometry to achieve this level of precision in measuring the Meissner effect. In order to do so, it's essential to optimize various parameters such as atomic velocity, measurement time, and atomic mass to maximize sensitivity. A detailed analysis including noise sources and limitations due to atomic physics is also included in this research. This study also explores potential applications of this measurement technique, including the analysis of local magnetic field expulsion from superconductors in quantum vortices and V-shaped samples. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finding allows the design of sub-10 nm gaps with excellent electron confinement for efficient spin-to-photon conversion. Furthermore, we demonstrate the importance of these considerations for the development of efficient spintronic devices.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, this work provides an overview of the strong normalization proofs in relation to the development of dependently typed programming languages and then discusses potential applications of legacy proof tools to legacy code, using Coq as an example. This survey ultimately concludes that, while the underlying principles of the various proofs exist, the actual proofs remain unclear due to their outdated nature and the lack of modern refinement. Therefore, completely reproving the strong normalization proof of the Calculus of Constructions in Coq appears feasible, albeit mainly in relation to the proof for the dependent intersection operator introduced by Paulin. This work positions such a reproof as a feasible outcome, given the ongoing advancements in proof refinement techniques visible in recent legacy proof reproufs, such as the reproof of the strong normalization proof for the Calculus of Constructions with dependent sum types and the reproof of the proof for the strong normalization of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions. This survey aims to provide a clear direction for researchers to undertake a reproof of the strong normalization proof for the Calculus of Constructions, considering the influence of dependent types such as dependent products and dependent intersections. This research is driven by the goal of creating a unified proof theory for dependent types that can be expressed through a type isomorphism from the dependent sum and product types to the dependent function type. This research is further motivated by the goal of creating formal proofs for the strong normalization property for various dependent types and the goal of creating a proof theory for dependent types through type isomorphisms. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  In addition, DynaSOAr's memory layout DSL and parallel data patterns library, which is compatible with common linear algebra and data-parallel programming frameworks, facilitate seamless integration with most GPU application frameworks, making it suitable for a wide range of high-performance computing applications.  We also include a case study where we applied DynaSOAr to the SO-AFFINE parallelization framework and successfully parallelized multiple objects within the FFT and MULI applications, resulting in significant performance improvements and enhanced memory usage.  In conclusion, the DynaSOAr CUDA framework provides an efficient and easy-to-use solution for easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming by facilitating the parallelization of SMMO applications with object structures, and we invite the research community to explore the capabilities of DynaSOAr with us.  The framework is now available for download at https://github.com/ajpcg/DynaSOAr. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. These predictions provide valuable insights into the YSR state structure and the influence of exchange and coupling effects on superconducting YSR states. Furthermore, the theoretical framework offers a useful tool for interpreting complex spectra of magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Our code and models are available on GitHub at https://github.com/yusodsFourierMask.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. To test this new perspective, we ran the S4J 3D reconstruction algorithm using a Monte Carlo solver and found that it can recover core properties such as size and optical thickness with reasonable accuracy, while also being robust against noise. These results provide a foundation for enhancing cloud tomographic reconstruction, particularly when using cloud imagers with higher spatial resolution, like future PLATON and ADITYA satellite systems. Nonetheless, refining algorithms and evaluating their performance through direct comparisons with actual cloud properties will be essential before cloud tomography can be applied from space. Despite the challenges, we believe this approach holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of cloud geometry and properties, especially when combined with cloud tomographic models trained on data from airbone measurements, such as used in the EACPS project. Finally, we suggest developing efficient 3D radiative transfer solvers and contributing them to open-source communities for use in cloud modeling and research. This way, scientists can engage in comparisons, validations, and adaptations of these solvers for various applications. Ultimately, this is a crucial step towards developing better cloud modeling and retrieval algorithms that can effectively handle complex convective clouds. This work is being presented as a extended abstract at the EACPS 2022 workshop. The full study is available as a companion paper at the journal submission. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, our study reveals that nitrogen defects are more stable in the anatase phase of TiO2, whereas carbon defects prefer the rutile phase.  Finally, we predict that both carbon and nitrogen defects will undergo lattice relaxation upon substitutional placement, with the formation of interstitial pairs requiring significantly more energy for nitrogen than carbon.  This research provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of carbon and nitrogen defects within TiO2, and offers potential avenues for further experimental and theoretical investigation.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I highlight that in the case of elastic top-quark pair production, limits on the scattering cross-section of $\sigma<0.36\,pb$ can be obtained, which is the most stringent limit on this process to date. All of these limits are derived without reliance on theoretical corrections for jet discrimination. Upgrading the current detector technology with a 120 $fs$ beam spot size would significantly improve the detectability of these top-quark pair production processes. Finally, I outline the potential for detecting rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ as well as top-quark pair production via the scattering process $\sigma=4\sigma pp\to tt$, both of which are anticipated to be feasible in the 13 TeV run at an LHC with 30 inverse abarns of data. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our findings also consider Ramsey numbers within colored graphs. To achieve this, we introduce a new relative upper density technique and a probabilistic argument to tackle 4-edge colored graphs. Furthermore, our results for cliques and odd cycles validate a conjecture made by Erdos and Galvin. This conjecture suggests that in every two-edge colored version of an infinitely large, densely enough constructed graph, there exists a densely enough constructed subgraph resembling $F$ with the same level of density. This holds true for structures like cliques and odd cycles of specific sizes. Our work thus provides a first look at this type of problem and paves the way for further investigation into upper density problems within Ramsey theory.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. In this work, measurement protocols that efficiently utilize multiple degrees of freedom are also explored, showcasing the potential for beyond-necessity noise resilience. Ultimately, our research proposes qudits as a more suitable system for ongoing quantum simulations, enabling a greater margin for error as we strive to achieve a more precise understanding of quantum dynamics.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. However, it's also worth noting that the magnitude of this effect may be mitigated by additional factors, potentially limiting its usefulness. Nevertheless, further exploration of this phenomenon through experimental and theoretical studies can provide greater insight into its implications. The proposed concept may also give rise to new possibilities for the observation of vacuum polarization effects, potentially facilitating the creation of high-density positron gases with unique properties. Moreover, it could also enable the development of intense, polarized positron beams, potentially enriching existing positron sources and opening up new avenues for particle physics research. Additionally, it may also give rise to new opportunities for the study of strong-field quantum electrodynamics, especially when coupled with theoretical simulations and interpretations. Ultimately, this phenomenon is expected to yield a deeper understanding of the interplay between intense laser fields, electron positron pairs, and the polarization properties of photons within dense materials. It's also worth considering that the proposed concept may have implications for the development of new sources of polarized positrons, positing the question of whether this could potentially contribute to enhanced sensitivity in experiments involving scattering processes, such as electron positron collisions, particularly when coupled with existing particle generation methods

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, this research introduces a new lower bound for the group's polynomial diameter based on its generating set size and complex irreducible characters, and it demonstrates that this lower bound is effective for a substantial number of groups with a polynomial diameter. This research also establishes the condition under which a group's diameter increases exponentially with the size of its generating set. This condition is met by groups with a non-archimedean property or those with a substantial normal subgroup with an exponentially large diameter. This research provides a new perspective on the relationship between a group's polynomial diameter and its expansion in the random walk. It also establishes the lower bound for the group's wavelength based on the diameter of its subgroup and the wavelength of the subgroup itself. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. We graphically represented these boundaries in the form of a magnetic energy ratio map. In this map, the region favored by stable magnetic fields is characterized by a magnetic energy ratio of approximately 1 to 4, with stable configurations preferring a gradual increase from the toroidal to the poloidal component. Additionally, we discovered that stable configurations are highly robust to changes in stable stratification, able to withstand a significant range of the ratio of the stellar radius to the scale height of the stratification. This finding suggests that stable magnetic fields in stars with moderate stratification could maintain their stability for an essentially infinite time. This research provides a long-sought theoretical framework for interpreting observational data on the magnetic fields of these stars. Furthermore, we propose using the energy ratio map as a diagnostic tool to identify stable magnetic fields in non-turbulent stellar interiors, and anticipate this framework to be applicable to additional types of stable magnetic fields generated through other interior processes. This research is a vital step towards a deeper understanding of the long-lasting magnetic fields of these stars. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories. Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options. Unlike traditional search engines that return random results based on queries, Pied Piper's unique approach ensures ordered results displaying the most suitable matches first. We've tested various deep learning models including the popular TransR and their music-specific variations, which incorporated NLP and audio features. Our findings reveal that using just the most relevant parts of the lyrics (known as subwords) or a middle section can enhance performance. Ultimately, our experiments yield promising outcomes using a custom-designed model that combines deep learning and Pied Piper's meta-search results, showcasing significant improvements over conventional search engine results and providing a stronger foundation for future music search engines to build upon. You can access our code and data at https://github.com/rahulda/PiedPiper. Our work addresses several key challenges, and we hope it will inspire further development in the pursuit of creating efficient and effective music search engines.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we find evidence suggesting that the massive star formation rate surface density within these clouds is significantly influenced by external factors, such as radiation pressure and wind shaping.  Finally, we observe a considerable gap in mass distribution between protostellar and starless cores, with a notable increase in the former's mass tail, indicating that extreme mass cores are more likely to give birth to massive stars.  This study's findings highlight the significance of infrared star formation surveys in discovering a population of massive protostellar cores that would have otherwise gone undetected through conventional submillimeter surveys.  Finally, we propose observing the core with an extreme mass distribution (>50 Solar Masses) candidate, called IRDC 17587-2647, which exhibits signs of core-collapse activity and may eventually give birth to a massive star.  This core-extrapolation model, which considers the cloud's motion and core mass function, suggests that up to three massive stars could be formed within the next 30,000 years as a result of core-collapse processes alone.  However, this prediction relies heavily on the core's mass and radius, as well as the specific physics that govern its further development, given that many factors, such as dust evolution and the influence of external stimuli, will shape its ultimate form.  Therefore, continuous and closely monitored observational data of this core and others like it are necessary to gain a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in its development and to provide insight into the broader implications of this study's findings. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. These results outflank similar representation theorems for intutionistic modal logics. The study also offers algebraic proofs of decidability and the finite model property for various Godel modal logics with operators. The results on decidability are then used to prove the decidability of canonical formulas for the basic Godel modal logic with one operator, a result that can be applied to show the first-order Godel modal logic with identity is decidable. The research also examines the complexity of the axiomatization of Godel modal logics with operators. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Moreover, we find that using contextual information yields higher accuracy rates across almost all feature engineering methods tested. Additionally, some techniques like kernel-based methods and neural networks prove sensitive to specific parameters and may not consistently achieve optimal results. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive examination of classification approaches for 3D LiDAR data, offering a foundation for further exploration and more complex scenarios involving multi-sensor data. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The direction of plate border curvature plays a significant role in determining stress patterns. Our findings provide a foundation for a comprehensive theory of friction in complex liquids and have implications for understanding avalanches in powers laws distributions. Additionally, our research offers potential explanations for the stick-slip motions observed in fluids over solid surfaces, as well as geological phenomena like earthquakes and granular flows. Besides, it also raises questions about the coexistence of stationary soap films and the stick-slip regime with negative work, which requires further exploration. Our study offers a perspective on the multi-scale nature of friction in complex liquids, involving interactions between a molecule's size, the curvature of Plateau borders, and a surface's dimensions. Consequently, this vision on the physics of complex liquids suggests that the field shares common features with other non-Newtonian fluids and demands a unique, combined experimental and theoretical approach to understand its intricacies. As such, we propose stress measurements in conjunction with visual observations as a viable method for exploring the physics of complex liquids at interfaces. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The behavior of the membrane is examined in greater detail in a pair of selected cross-sectional views, with the resulting state determined by a combination of both local conditions near the point of origin as well as the membrane's connection to the boundary that confines it. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We've also derived an expression for average dissipated energy in terms of an equilibrium correlation energy, revealing that it serves as a fundamental property that can't be altered by the expansion process. We further demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by investigating the dynamics of a harmonic oscillator and its thermal fluctuations, comparing our findings with predictions made by using nonequilibrium ensemble methods. These breakthroughs will enable researchers to examine the dynamics of complex systems and investigate new phenomena arising from the interplay between internal vibrations and thermal fluctuations. Ultimately, we believe that extending microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics to complex systems and macroscopic systems will provide a comprehensive understanding of thermodynamic systems, advancing the field and shedding new light on fundamental principles. We also introduce a new parameter, entropy production time, as a coherent measure of dissipation in oscillating systems, and we anticipate that it will become a valuable benchmark in analyzing nonequilibrium dynamics. By applying these methods, we can finally study the kinetics of phase transitions, evaluating entropy production and microwork in highly nonlinear systems, such as the double well oscillator with a moving wall, and comparing our findings with numerical simulations. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed models also achieve superior performance without additional training data or noise. We also analyze the look-ahead attention's ability to capture target word relationships and present visual examples of target sentence generations using our model. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Finally, we discuss potential challenges and opportunities for the future of this field, highlighting the potential for a strong connection between advances in translational computer science and successful implementation of large-scale software projects. In addition, we believe that taking a translational perspective is essential for computer scientists to effectively address complex, real-world problems in science and engineering. In conclusion, we hope that our experience with grid computing and the Globus Toolkit can serve as an inspiring example for other projects in the field of translational computer science. It is possible that the most significant difficulty in tackling such projects will be finding suitable applications for research, rather than conducting the research itself. In the future, we anticipate that computer scientists will face increased pressure to deliver working software that solves significant problems, and that this delivery orientation will become the primary focus of computer science in the eyes of potential students, academics, and industrial practitioners. It is our hope that, in response, the computer science community will emphasize the value of applying research directly, making a strong case for it in the eyes of academics, and providing students with a well-rounded education that includes a focus on delivering working software. It is only through this education and by making a strong case for it that the community will be able to attract top talent to this area, who can deliver working software that solves significant problems, and address various challenges facing the field. It is our hope that future researchers will build upon the progress made in grid computing and the Globus Toolkit, and make significant contributions to the area of translational computer science. It is our hope that future grid computing and HPC researchers and developers will build upon the progress made in grid computing and the Globus Toolkit, and make significant contributions to the area of translational computer science. It is our hope that future researchers and developers in this area will have a focus on delivering working software that solves significant problems, and address various challenges facing the field

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  We believe that our research will motivate the scientific community to explore the design of computer-supported collaborative learning environments that can identify and respond to curiosity in action.  This study is part of the ISCS CLARITY project that aims to design computer-supported collaborative learning environments that can identify and respond to curiosity in action.  We are sharing our research findings with the larger scientific community in the hope that it will motivate the design of computer programs that can recognize and stimulate curiosity in real-life scenarios.  We are seeking feedback from the scientific community as well as input from psychologists and education experts that will guide the next stage of our research.  We are particularly interested in feedback on our theoretical framework and our approach to designing computer programs that can identify and stimulate curiosity in real-time.  We are also seeking to collaborate with researchers and education experts that can contribute to our work.  We are sharing the source code of our pilot application that demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in stimulating curiosity in real-time.  We are looking for feedback on our source code as well as input on how to move forward with the next stage of our research.  We are particularly interested in feedback on the following issues:  - Whether our theoretical framework for curiosity in collaborative learning settings is comprehensive and valid.  - What other behaviors besides the ones we identified

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is further underscored by an open-source implementation that is freely accessible. This implementation not only facilitates the evaluation of these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes by providing a flexible toolkit that is simple to use but also enables the creation of various graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes based on distinct undirected graph topologies. This implementation also includes a suite of tools that can be utilized to enhance the performance of these models, including methods that address scalability and model selection challenges. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, optimization of routing results in efficient operation of ridesharing vehicles with minimal overlap in monitoring areas. A reliability-based threshold approach is also introduced and found to enhance coverage and reliability further. Our findings provide a foundation for utilizing fleet mobile sensing to effectively monitor and manage urban road conditions. A research extension is also presented for considering time-dependent traffic data in routing optimization, with potential for future exploration. The developed approach and conclusions are supported by comprehensive numerical and realistic data-based analysis. The associated algorithm and data are available for study and replication through an open online repository. The innovative mobile sensing approach and associated algorithmic solutions can contribute to optimized routing and efficient maintenance of urban roads. Moreover, the approach provides valuable data for improved traffic management and informed urban planning strategies. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the utilization of ride-sharing vehicle data in addressing various urban challenges. The concepts presented can be extended for consideration in contexts beyond fleet mobile sensing. The research offers a theoretical and practical framework that can be expanded for exploration of additional ideas within this domain. The associated algorithm and data are available for further analysis and replication through an open online repository. The innovative mobile sensing approach and associated algorithmic solutions can contribute to optimized routing and efficient maintenance of urban roads.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Additionally, we found that J/ψ decay into a neutrino pair can contribute to existing constraints on certain effective operators, specifically those with an invisible photon decay channel. In the context of a comprehensive analysis that also considers direct detection and neutrino physics, our findings indicate that J/ψ invisible decays can slightly tighten existing limits on light dark matter or contribute marginally to neutrino constraints, depending on the specific model and parameter settings. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we verify that our new methods outperform existing uniform SGLMs under similar conditions. Further, we successfully apply our algorithm to solve a real-world epidemiological model described by delay differential equations. The implementation of this model and the convergence of our new SGLMs are confirmed by numerical results. Our algorithm is publicly available under the name SGLMVariableStepsize at numdige.github.io/algorithm/sglmvariablestepsize.html.

Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for exploring variable stepsize SGLMs on uniform grids and further research opportunities.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Our findings are relevant not only to the specific autoscoring models investigated but also to any other complex, high-stakes decision-making systems that operate in similar closed systems. Furthermore, our study introduces a new evaluation metric called the Score Stability Index (SSI) that is useful for assessing the robustness of such systems. The code for our analysis and proposed solutions is available at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/Probing-Automated-Scoring. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development and deployment of similar high-stakes automated decision systems. The study's results highlight the importance of understanding the complex workings of these algorithms and the need to ensure their reliability and stability in high-stakes applications. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. As a result, the source can produce plasma with densities of up to 1.3 x 10^20 molecules per cubic meter. Further enhancements to the source have been proposed, including the use of a better antenna and various modifications to increase plasma density along the centerline. It is anticipated that with these improvements, the source will be capable of producing plasma with densities of up to 1.5 x 10^20 molecules per cubic meter. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the W-shaped network is designed as a nested, bi-directional neural network. By operating on density masks, which represent the density and shape of objects, rather than one-hot masks, which represent both object density and background density, the model's performance is significantly enhanced. Furthermore, the model is trained on density masks, rather than one-hot masks, in order to focus directly on object density and shape. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Through this combined effort, we aim to inform superior treatment strategies for COVID-19 by examining how inflammation's varied causes respond to treatment. Ultimately, our goal is to utilize this integrated framework to guide prospective experiments, providing valuable data that can enhance the model and, in turn, contribute to the development of more effective treatment approaches for COVID-19. This combined initiative between computational simulations and experimental research will provide valuable new data on the host-dynamics of COVID-19, leading to better treatment strategies and informing superior protocols for future experiments. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed method achieves greater flexibility, enabling the enhancement of various CT images with different doses. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/achinze01/Matrix-Model-Based-RL.

reinforcement learning, using shared dynamics models may not always be beneficial.
