In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our study demonstrated that using artificial intelligence for this task could be a viable option, and we made specific recommendations for implementing this approach successfully. Additionally, we made all training data, implementation details, and trial codes publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. The key advantage of this approach is that it allows for flexible implementation and easily interoperable training with existing imaging reconstruction models. The seamless integration of the GAN and model can significantly simplify training and significantly reduce the necessary training data size. The methodology we proposed is versatile and easy to implement, and we have made the code publicly available.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude by discussing the crucial role that invariant manifolds play in the analysis of dynamical systems and the importance of further research in this field.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, the results provide evidence that screen velocities can differ significantly from pulsar velocities. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a subjective test confirms that QPNet can generate clinically relevant speech with a natural quality. The source codes are available at https://github.com/ghulghule/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system. We found that MADARi's annotation guidelines
and interface aids annotators in their task, yet dialect-specific difficulties persist.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. As a result, further research is needed to address this limitation. The developed method is implemented in the open-source software package Adfront, available for download and use.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

Furthermore, we found that the D-poor water with hydrogen isotopic values ranging from -444 to -56.9 originated from nebular hydrogen, and could have contributed 154-311 ppm of water to the pyroxene minerals, while the remaining water with high D values may have originated from the reduction of metallic iron during the formation of the asteroid. 

In addition, our research provided new constraints for the formation of chondrite, and indicated that the formation of chondrite must occur within a few million years to explain the D-poor hydrogen isotopic values, and that the formation of the asteroid should involve the reduction of metallic iron to obtain water with D values higher than -70. 

Our analysis also highlighted the importance of reducing metallic iron to obtain water with D values higher than -70, and suggested that this process occurs simultaneously with the formation of the asteroid.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the benefits of zero-shot learning for speech-to-text in new language pairs. We also observe the capability of these models to handle pairs that weren't exposed during training but share similarities with trained pairs, such as Spanish to Portuguese. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our model reveals that the scattering cross-section and optical force can significantly differ between the Mie and dipolar regimes, especially in the case of metallic particles. We also observe that modeling particle arrays using spherical multipoles can be more efficient than simulated annealing. Moreover, our results indicate that the particle's material properties have a significant impact on its optical force, with silicon experiencing the strongest force due to its large refractive index. Finally, our method can be applied to model particle pairs, demonstrating that spherical multipoles provide a useful tool for understanding the optical force acting on particles across various wavelengths.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, algebraic limit passage towards U(gl(n)) is attainable through Olshanski decomposition and filtered algebra direct and inverse limits. This research thus extends upon existing knowledge by incorporating representation theoretic aspects within the framework of Olshanski decomposition and direct/inverse limits, revealing new insights into the structure of algebras and representation categories through the central Schur elements/quantum immanants, a practice inheritable to other simple Lie algebras. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Meanwhile, some radiatively generated "solar" parameters can lead to significant effects on this process. Meanwhile, certain models on the edge of viability can be on the verge of validating upcoming experiments for this decay. Nonetheless, the ability to discover or rule out the simplest scoto-seesaw model relies largely on direct dark matter detection. Finally, we identify potential lines of investigation to further explore this theory's implications within its newly defined parameter context.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The developed framework is also applicable to other $d$-shell systems with complex orbital structures in cubic symmetry. To illustrate this, we reevaluate experimental branching ratios in SrCu$_2(OD)_2NCS$ and Ti$_2(OH)_6NCS$, and suggest that intermediate electron-electron coupling justifies somewhat mixed $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital states in these materials. Finally, we propose that strategic manipulation of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can provide a new pathway for designing materials with desired orbital ground states and associated phenomena.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. This work has been recognized as an outstanding paper by the organizing committee. In addition, our researchers were awarded the Best Paper Honorable Mention for developing an innovative technique in medical imaging analysis. This research was supported by Siemens Healthineers, the National Institute of Health (R01EB017240), and the National Science Foundation (IIS-1838154). Our technique demonstrates substantial potential for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement and organ transference. Nonetheless, it is crucial to note that the current implementation is not suitable for real-world clinical applications due to its limited scalability and precision. In order to advance this research, we are making our code freely available for the community to contribute and improve. This initiative aims to facilitate collaboration and address existing challenges. In particular, we face the following difficulties that require further exploration: (1) enhancing the ability of the generator to produce a wide range of medical images, (2) improving the accuracy of the encoder in reconstructing organ structures, (3) developing a more efficient and adaptable technique for different datasets, and (4) addressing the challenge of transference across different patient populations. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments.
